title: Dual-Platform Precision Measurement of the $3^2D_{5/2}$ to $4^2S_{1/2}$ $g$-Factor Ratio in $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$
summary: We report precision measurements of the ratio of Landé $g$ factors between the $3^2D_{5/2}$ and $4^2S_{1/2}$ states of a single trapped $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$ ion. The measurements are performed in two distinct ion trap apparatus: a cryogenic surface electrode radiofrequency Paul trap and a room-temperature permanent magnet Penning trap. The Penning trap measurements yield a ratio of $0.599~488~813~3(2)$, which represents a more than 40-fold uncertainty reduction compared to previous work. The radiofrequency trap measurement yields a concurring value of $0.599~488~813(6)$. We estimate that systematic shifts for each system are well below the respective statistical uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Precision measurements of the Landé g-factor ratio between the 3²D₅/₂ and 4²S₁/₂ states of a single trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ion were performed in two distinct ion traps (cryogenic surface-electrode Paul trap and room-temperature Penning trap), achieving a 40-fold uncertainty reduction in the Penning trap measurement with concurring results from the Paul trap.
AI.motivation: To achieve high-precision measurements of the Landé g-factor ratio in ⁴⁰Ca⁺, reducing uncertainty by over 40-fold compared to previous work, using two complementary trapping platforms to cross-validate results and constrain systematic effects.
AI.method: Measurements were conducted in two distinct apparatus: a cryogenic surface-electrode radiofrequency Paul trap and a room-temperature permanent magnet Penning trap. The ratio of g-factors between the 3²D₅/₂ and 4²S₁/₂ states was extracted from precision spectroscopy on a single trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ion in each system.
AI.result: Penning trap: g-factor ratio = 0.5994888133(2). RF Paul trap: g-factor ratio = 0.599488813(6). The Penning trap result represents a >40-fold reduction in uncertainty versus prior work. Systematic shifts were estimated to be well below the respective statistical uncertainties for both systems.
AI.conclusion: The two independent measurements concur, demonstrating robust cross-platform verification of the g-factor ratio. The achieved precision enables improved tests of quantum electrodynamics and determinations of fundamental constants in atomic systems.

title: Theoretical ab initio Evolution of Satellite Intensity near Threshold for Cu K-shell transitions
summary: In this work, we have investigated the evolution of satellite intensity near the ionization threshold for Cu K-shell transitions through theoretical methods. Employing standard state-of-the-art ab initio methods, we have calculated all Cu K-shell transitions and simulated the full K$α_1$ and K$α_2$ spectrum where all transition parameters, as well as shake probabilities were determined theoretically. Through these calculations we show that standard state-of-the-art ab initio methods achieve good agreement with experiment and enable us to simulate the intensity evolution near ionization thresholds within a good margin of error. Below-threshold satellite intensity was found to originate from resonant 1s$\rightarrow$3d and 1s$\rightarrow$4p excitations in Cu(I) and Cu(II) oxide phases respectively, which were included in our simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ab initio methods to calculate Cu K-shell transitions and simulate Kα₁ and Kα₂ spectra, achieving good agreement with experiment and explaining below-threshold satellite intensity as originating from resonant 1s→3d and 1s→4p excitations in Cu(I) and Cu(II) oxide phases.
AI.motivation: To investigate the evolution of satellite intensity near the ionization threshold for Cu K-shell transitions using theoretical methods, aiming to understand the origins of below-threshold satellite features.
AI.method: Standard state-of-the-art ab initio methods were used to calculate all Cu K-shell transitions and simulate the full Kα₁ and Kα₂ spectrum, with all transition parameters and shake probabilities determined theoretically.
AI.result: The ab initio methods achieved good agreement with experiment, enabling simulation of intensity evolution near ionization thresholds within a good margin of error. Below-threshold satellite intensity was attributed to resonant 1s→3d excitations in Cu(I) oxide and 1s→4p excitations in Cu(II) oxide phases.
AI.conclusion: Standard state-of-the-art ab initio methods are effective for simulating Cu K-shell satellite intensity evolution near ionization thresholds, and the origin of below-threshold satellites is identified as specific resonant excitations in different copper oxide phases.

title: Extracting inter-nuclear distances in the oxygen molecule interacting with an XFEL-pulse: a fundamental system for understanding Coulomb explosion imaging
summary: We investigate the interaction of O$_{2}$ with an X-ray Free Electron laser (XFEL) pulse of short duration. We consider a photon energy of 570 eV, which allows for the formation of molecular states with up to two core holes. We compute the sum of the final kinetic energies, i.e. the kinetic energy release (KER) of the atomic fragments for different fragmentation channels. We demonstrate that with the knowledge of the potential energy curves the equilibrium inter-nuclear distance of O$_{2}$ is best extracted from the O$^{+}$+O$^{+}$ channel and not from higher-charged channels such as O$^{2+}$+O$^{2+}$. This challenges our current understanding of Coulomb explosion imaging, where from just applying quasi-classical dynamics one expects that the equilibrium inter-nuclear distance of molecules is best extracted from higher-charged fragmentation channels. On the other hand, we show that the KER of the O$^{+}$+O$^{+}$ channel is inconsistent with the one obtained by just calculating the Coulomb repulsion of the atomic fragments resulting from molecular dissociation.

AI.tldr: This study investigates O₂ interaction with XFEL pulses (570 eV) and finds that the equilibrium inter-nuclear distance of O₂ is best extracted from the O⁺+O⁺ fragmentation channel, not higher-charged channels, challenging conventional Coulomb explosion imaging assumptions.
AI.motivation: To investigate how O₂ interacts with XFEL pulses at 570 eV and determine which fragmentation channel best reveals the equilibrium inter-nuclear distance, challenging the conventional Coulomb explosion imaging approach that favors higher-charged channels.
AI.method: Computational study at photon energy 570 eV allowing formation of molecular states with up to two core holes, calculating kinetic energy release (KER) of atomic fragments across different fragmentation channels.
AI.result: The O⁺+O⁺ channel provides the best extraction of equilibrium inter-nuclear distance, contrary to expectations that higher-charged channels (e.g., O²⁺+O²⁺) would be optimal. Additionally, the KER from O⁺+O⁺ channel is inconsistent with pure Coulomb repulsion calculations.
AI.conclusion: Standard quasi-classical assumptions about Coulomb explosion imaging are challenged; lower-charged fragmentation channels can be more informative for structural measurements, and simple Coulomb repulsion models are insufficient for interpreting O⁺+O⁺ KER data.

title: Efficient photo-ionizing elimination of detrimental electric fields for Rydberg atoms
summary: Rydberg atoms are highly sensitive to external electric fields due to their exaggerated electronic properties. This unique feature lays the foundation for many of their applications in quantum science. However, an uncontrolled stray electric field can be detrimental, severely degrading their quantum control. In this work, we demonstrate a universal scheme that relies on the efficient creation of an in-vacuum plasma source by photo-ionizing laser-cooled atoms to eliminate detrimental electric fields in a Rydberg-atom tweezer array platform, requiring only readily available resources. With this method, we began with a Stark-ionized Rydberg continuum spectrum caused by a large, unknown stray electric field and ultimately recovered stable, coherent excitation of an individual Rydberg state after fully eliminating the field. Our method is directly applicable to existing Rydberg-atom platforms and can also be useful in other experiments sensitive to stray electric fields.

AI.tldr: A universal method using photo-ionized laser-cooled atoms to create an in-vacuum plasma source eliminates stray electric fields in Rydberg-atom tweezer arrays, recovering stable coherent Rydberg excitation from a Stark-ionized continuum.
AI.motivation: Stray electric fields severely degrade quantum control of Rydberg atoms, which are highly sensitive to external fields due to their exaggerated electronic properties.
AI.method: Creating an in-vacuum plasma source via photo-ionization of laser-cooled atoms to eliminate stray electric fields in a Rydberg-atom tweezer array platform.
AI.result: Transitioned from a Stark-ionized Rydberg continuum spectrum caused by large unknown stray fields to stable, coherent excitation of an individual Rydberg state after full field elimination.
AI.conclusion: The method is universal, directly applicable to existing Rydberg-atom platforms, and useful for other experiments sensitive to stray electric fields.

title: Universality and Dynamical Inequivalence in Isospectral Non-Hermitian Anderson Transitions
summary: The Hatano Nelson paradigm establishes that extensive bulk nonreciprocity can destabilize Anderson localization via an imaginary gauge flux. Here, we demonstrate that extensive nonreciprocity is not a necessary ingredient: a single non-Hermitian boundary bond in a disordered one-dimensional ring suffices to drive the localization-delocalization transition. More generally, we construct an exactly isospectral family of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that continuously interpolates between the uniform Hatano Nelson model and the single-bond limit. We show that the universal critical behavior encompassing spectral, eigenstate, and topological diagnostics is gauge invariant and governed solely by the total imaginary gauge flux, regardless of its spatial distribution. Remarkably, despite sharing identical spectra and critical exponents, different configurations within this isospectral family exhibit qualitatively distinct quantum dynamics, establishing a fundamental separation between static and dynamical universality in non-Hermitian systems. Specifically, the single boundary realization features rapid operator scrambling, oscillatory wavepacket acceleration, and a double re-entrant steady state entanglement transition. Finally, we propose an experimentally feasible realization based on multi-terminal topological transport, providing a realistic route toward observing boundary induced non Hermitian criticality and its unconventional dynamical signatures.

AI.tldr: A single non-Hermitian boundary bond in a disordered 1D ring suffices to drive the localization-delocalization transition, establishing that extensive bulk nonreciprocity is not necessary. The critical behavior depends only on total imaginary gauge flux, not its spatial distribution. Despite shared spectra and critical exponents, different isospectral configurations show qualitatively distinct dynamics (scrambling, acceleration, re-entrant entanglement transitions).
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing Hatano-Nelson paradigm that extensive bulk nonreciprocity is required to destabilize Anderson localization, and to investigate whether a minimal non-Hermitian boundary perturbation can drive the same transition.
AI.method: Constructs an exactly isospectral family of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians interpolating between the uniform Hatano-Nelson model and a single-bond boundary limit. Analyzes spectral, eigenstate, and topological diagnostics to establish gauge-invariant universal critical behavior.
AI.result: The localization-delocalization transition is driven solely by total imaginary gauge flux irrespective of spatial distribution. Isospectral configurations exhibit identical critical exponents but qualitatively distinct dynamics (operator scrambling, oscillatory wavepacket acceleration, double re-entrant steady state entanglement transition).
AI.conclusion: Static and dynamical universality are fundamentally separated in non-Hermitian systems. The single boundary bond realization offers a feasible experimental route via multi-terminal topological transport.

title: A Puck-informed mode-resolved phase-field fatigue framework for unidirectional composites
summary: Fatigue fracture in unidirectional fibre-reinforced composites is strongly mode dependent: transverse and off-axis cycling is governed by matrix and inter-fibre mechanisms, whereas fibre-aligned cycling activates a longitudinal channel with a higher fracture-energy scale and a different crack topology. Single-damage-variable models can fit global stiffness loss but cannot identify the active mechanism. This work proposes a Puck-informed, mode-resolved phase-field fatigue framework with separate channels for fibre-dominated and matrix/inter-fibre fatigue. Each channel has its own fatigue history, threshold, and resistance-degradation law. Fatigue does not directly degrade elastic stiffness; it lowers the fracture resistance of the active channel, while the corresponding phase field controls stiffness loss and crack-path evolution. The formulation is implemented in Abaqus/Standard using a compact UMAT-UEL architecture with one orthotropic mechanical routine and two scalar phase-field layers. Using one fixed IM7/8552 material and fatigue card, the model is verified through one-element tests, parameter sweeps, and centred-notch and open-hole tension cases at 0, 45, and 90 degrees under monotonic and cyclic loading. Without orientation- or geometry-specific tuning, the framework reproduces transverse matrix/inter-fibre cracking at 90 degrees, off-axis cracking at 45 degrees, and longitudinal matrix splitting with delayed fibre activation at 0 degrees. The fatigue lives follow the expected ordering: 45- and 90-degree cases fail within about 1,000 cycles, while 0-degree cases run out to 200,000 cycles without fibre cracking. Additional load, hole-size, mesh, length-scale, and cycle-block studies confirm consistent crack modes and converged trends. The study is a numerical verification and cross-geometry consistency assessment, not a calibrated experimental life-prediction claim.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Puck-informed, mode-resolved phase-field fatigue framework for unidirectional fibre-reinforced composites, with separate damage channels for fibre-dominated and matrix/inter-fibre fatigue. Verified through various numerical tests, the model reproduces mode-dependent cracking and correct fatigue-life ordering without orientation- or geometry-specific tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing single-damage-variable models can fit global stiffness loss but cannot identify the active fatigue mechanism (fibre vs. matrix/inter-fibre), which is critical given the strong mode dependence of fatigue fracture in unidirectional composites.
AI.method: A phase-field fatigue framework with two separate damage channels (fibre and matrix/inter-fibre), each with its own fatigue history, threshold, and resistance-degradation law. Fatigue lowers fracture resistance of the active channel, while the phase field controls stiffness loss and crack-path evolution. Implemented in Abaqus/Standard using a UMAT-UEL architecture.
AI.result: Without orientation- or geometry-specific tuning, the model reproduces transverse matrix cracking (90°), off-axis cracking (45°), and longitudinal matrix splitting with delayed fibre activation (0°). Fatigue lives follow expected ordering: 45°/90° fail within ~1,000 cycles, 0° cases run to 200,000 cycles without fibre cracking. Consistent crack modes and converged trends across load, hole-size, mesh, length-scale, and cycle-block studies.
AI.conclusion: The study provides numerical verification and cross-geometry consistency assessment of the proposed framework, though it is not a calibrated experimental life-prediction claim.

title: Seven- and eight-loop critical exponents of the three-dimensional Ising model
summary: We determine the critical exponents $η$, $ν$, and the correction-to-scaling exponent $ω$ of the three-dimensional Ising universality class by resumming the recently computed seven- and eight-loop renormalization-group series in the $ε=4-d$ expansion (O.~Schnetz, \textit{Phys. Rev. D} \textbf{97}, 085018 (2018); O.~Schnetz, \textit{Phys. Rev. D} \textbf{107}, 036002 (2023)). The resummation combines conformal mapping with a homographic transformation, while the resummation parameters are optimized according to two complementary criteria. This approach yields precise estimates of the critical exponents together with quantitative uncertainty estimates. We find that the error bar on $η$ decreases rapidly with increasing loop order, whereas this is the case neither for $ν$ nor for $ω$. Unexpectedly, although the estimated values are accurate in absolute terms, their slow convergence with the loop order leads to a slight but systematic tension with the conformal bootstrap estimates that are currently considered as the benchmark. We discuss several possible origins of this behavior and its implications for high-order resummations of perturbative renormalization-group series.

AI.tldr: This paper resums seven- and eight-loop ε-expansion series to compute critical exponents η, ν, and ω for the 3D Ising universality class. While error bars for η decrease rapidly with loop order, ν and ω converge slowly, leading to systematic tension with conformal bootstrap benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve estimates of critical exponents for the 3D Ising universality class by leveraging newly available high-loop (seven- and eight-loop) renormalization-group series in the ε=4-d expansion, and to investigate convergence behavior and potential discrepancies with other high-precision methods like conformal bootstrap.
AI.method: Resummation of seven- and eight-loop ε-expansion series using conformal mapping combined with a homographic transformation; resummation parameters optimized via two complementary criteria to provide quantitative uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: Precise estimates of η, ν, and ω are obtained. The error bar on η decreases rapidly with loop order, while ν and ω do not exhibit the same convergence speed. Despite accurate absolute values, systematic tension with conformal bootstrap estimates is observed.
AI.conclusion: High-order resummations of perturbative RG series show differential convergence across exponents. The systematic tension with conformal bootstrap suggests either limitations of the resummation approach or unresolved issues in the series, motivating further investigation into high-order resummation techniques.

title: Atomistic Modeling for Electro-chemical Reactions
summary: Computational modeling plays a central role in advancing our understanding of electro-chemical reactions and may thus guide the rational development of sustainable energy technologies. Despite significant methodological progress, achieving predictive and quantitatively reliable simulations of electrified solid-liquid interfaces under operando conditions remains a major challenge. Recently, the European COST Action EU-CONCERT (EUropean COllaborative Network on electroCatalysis for Efficient Renewable Technologies) was launched with the aim of advancing atomistic modeling of electrochemical reactions through systematic benchmarking and cross-validation. This position paper outlines the consortium's view of the current state of the art, identifies the priority methodological challenges to be addressed, and defines the benchmark tests that are urgently needed. This paper should serve as a guide to the community and a roadmap for the EU-CONCERT COST Action.

AI.tldr: This position paper from the EU-CONCERT COST Action outlines the current state, priority challenges, and benchmark tests needed to advance predictive atomistic modeling of electrified solid-liquid interfaces for electrochemical reactions, serving as a roadmap for the community.
AI.motivation: Despite significant methodological progress in computational modeling of electro-chemical reactions, achieving predictive and quantitatively reliable simulations of electrified solid-liquid interfaces under operando conditions remains a major challenge, hindering rational development of sustainable energy technologies.
AI.method: The EU-CONCERT COST Action was launched to advance atomistic modeling through systematic benchmarking and cross-validation. This position paper synthesizes the consortium's view of the current state of the art, identifies priority methodological challenges, and defines urgently needed benchmark tests.
AI.result: The paper identifies specific priority methodological challenges and defines benchmark tests that are urgently needed for advancing the field, serving as both a guide to the community and a roadmap for the EU-CONCERT COST Action.
AI.conclusion: Systematic benchmarking and cross-validation through collaborative networks like EU-CONCERT are essential to overcome the challenge of predictive simulations of electrified interfaces, and this paper provides the roadmap to guide such coordinated efforts.

title: Lecture notes on random matrix theory: the results, the applications, and the analytical tools
summary: Random matrix theory has established itself as a theoretical cornerstone of the mathematical sciences over the past century. It has undeniable utility in areas of research as diverse as nuclear physics, finance, ecology and disordered systems. The purpose of these notes is twofold. First, the most famous and widely used classic results are derived in a pedagogical manner, mostly using the comparatively elementary and transparent cavity method. The significance of each result is then demonstrated in the context of a particular application. There are also some select exercises at the end of each section. In the second part of these notes, a reference guide of analytical techniques for the random-matrix/disordered-systems practitioner is provided. Introducing the diagrammatic, replica, path-integral, and supersymmetric formalisms from first principles, we rederive some of the aforementioned classic results, particularly focussing on the simplest one -- the semicircle law. Innovations such as the population dynamics method and the tools of free probability theory are also included. We discuss the merits of each analytical approach, and we highlight the contexts in which each becomes particularly useful.

AI.tldr: These notes provide a pedagogical introduction to random matrix theory, deriving classic results using the cavity method and demonstrating applications, then offering a reference guide to advanced analytical techniques (diagrammatic, replica, path-integral, supersymmetric, population dynamics, free probability) with a focus on the semicircle law.
AI.motivation: To provide a pedagogical yet comprehensive introduction to random matrix theory that bridges classic results and modern analytical techniques, making the field accessible to practitioners across diverse disciplines.
AI.method: The paper uses the cavity method for deriving classic results pedagogically, and then introduces diagrammatic, replica, path-integral, supersymmetric formalisms, population dynamics, and free probability for advanced analysis, with the semicircle law as the primary example.
AI.result: A two-part pedagogical reference: (1) classic RMT results derived via the cavity method with applications and exercises; (2) a guide to six advanced analytical techniques for random matrix and disordered systems, all applied to rederive the semicircle law.
AI.conclusion: The notes serve both as a pedagogical introduction to classic RMT results and as a practical reference guide comparing the merits of various analytical approaches, helping practitioners choose the right technique for their context.

title: Parity Anomaly of Preformed Pairs Governs the Thermal Hall Effect above $T_c$
summary: A large negative thermal Hall signal has been reported across multiple cuprate families in the pseudogap phase where the superconducting order parameter has vanished, with a magnitude that no existing microscopic theory reproduces without free parameters. Competing proposals based on chiral phonons, spinons, or loop currents each require undetermined coupling constants and do not predict the temperature dependence in terms of an independently measured spectroscopic gap. We show that the parity anomaly of $(2+1)$-dimensional quantum field theory resolves this long-standing puzzle: the preformed-pair pseudogap $Δ_{\rm pg}(T)$ enters the parity-odd fermion determinant identically to a condensate mass, yielding the exact parameter-free formula $κ_{xy}/T = (π^2 k_B^2/6h)\,C\,\tanh[Δ_{\rm pg}(T)/(2k_BT)]$, where $C$ is the Chern number of the chiral pairing channel and $Δ_{\rm pg}(T)$ is directly measurable by ARPES or STM. Coleman-Hill non-renormalization protects the result against higher-loop corrections, and two independent numerical tests, Wilson-loop flux threading and DMRG on $p+ip$ cylinders, confirm the anomaly correlation length to $0.2\%$ accuracy with no power-law finite-size corrections. The theory predicts thermal Hall onset at $T^*$ rather than $T_c$, provides a falsifiable logarithmic-derivative test against ARPES data, and yields a concrete quantitative target for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the long-standing puzzle of large negative thermal Hall signals in cuprate pseudogap phases by showing that the parity anomaly of (2+1)-D quantum field theory yields an exact parameter-free formula where the preformed-pair pseudogap enters identically to a condensate mass.
AI.motivation: A large negative thermal Hall signal observed across multiple cuprate families in the pseudogap phase cannot be reproduced by existing microscopic theories without free parameters, and competing proposals (chiral phonons, spinons, loop currents) require undetermined coupling constants and fail to predict the temperature dependence from independently measured spectroscopic gaps.
AI.method: The authors apply the parity anomaly of (2+1)-D quantum field theory, showing the preformed-pair pseudogap Δ_pg(T) enters the parity-odd fermion determinant identically to a condensate mass. They derive an exact parameter-free formula κ_xy/T = (π²k_B²/6h)·C·tanh[Δ_pg(T)/(2k_BT)], where C is the Chern number. Coleman-Hill non-renormalization protects against higher-loop corrections. Two independent numerical tests (Wilson-loop flux threading and DMRG on p+ip cylinders) confirm the anomaly correlation length to 0.2% accuracy.
AI.result: The theory reproduces the thermal Hall signal without free parameters, predicts thermal Hall onset at T^* rather than T_c, provides a falsifiable logarithmic-derivative test against ARPES data, and yields a concrete quantitative target for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. Numerical confirmation shows 0.2% accuracy with no power-law finite-size corrections.
AI.conclusion: The parity anomaly of (2+1)-D QFT provides the correct theoretical framework for understanding the pseudogap thermal Hall effect in cuprates, with parameter-free predictions directly testable by ARPES, STM, and twisted bilayer graphene experiments.

title: NSF Future Manufacturing Data Challenge: A Multimodal DED Dataset for Probabilistic Local Geometry Prediction in Laser Tracks
summary: We introduce a multimodal directed energy deposition (DED) dataset for predicting the probabilistic local geometric variation of single laser tracks produced on stainless-steel 316L substrates. The dataset supports the NSF Future Manufacturing Data Challenge and contains three complementary modalities: in-situ thermal image sequences from a Stratonics ThermaViz melt-pool sensor, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images acquired using a Zeiss EVO MA10 system, and full-field height maps acquired using a Bruker ContourGT-K white-light 3D optical profilometer. Each experiment is a bead-on-plate scan at one of four laser powers, 200, 300, 350, and 400 W, with a fixed scan speed of 10 mm/s. The release includes starter notebooks, participant-facing code, and a multimodal coordinate convention that links thermal, SEM, and height-map measurements over a common physical 20-100 mm window.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multimodal DED dataset with in-situ thermal imaging, SEM, and profilometry data for predicting probabilistic geometric variation in single laser tracks on stainless-steel 316L substrates, supporting the NSF Future Manufacturing Data Challenge.
AI.motivation: To support the NSF Future Manufacturing Data Challenge by providing a multimodal dataset that enables probabilistic prediction of local geometric variation in directed energy deposition additive manufacturing processes.
AI.method: Three complementary modalities were collected: in-situ thermal image sequences from a Stratonics ThermaViz melt-pool sensor, SEM images from a Zeiss EVO MA10 system, and full-field height maps from a Bruker ContourGT-K white-light 3D optical profilometer. Experiments were bead-on-plate scans at four laser powers (200, 300, 350, 400 W) with a fixed scan speed of 10 mm/s. Starter notebooks and a multimodal coordinate convention linking measurements over a 20-100 mm window are provided.
AI.result: A multimodal DED dataset containing thermal, SEM, and height-map data across four laser power conditions, with aligned coordinate conventions and reusable code for the research community.
AI.conclusion: This dataset enables probabilistic modeling of geometric variation in DED processes and serves as a benchmark resource for the NSF Future Manufacturing Data Challenge.

title: Anisotropic vacancy-induced magnetization textures in altermagnets
summary: We study magnetic textures induced by vacancies in altermagnets using microscopic simulations and low-energy field theory. We show that a vacancy generically produces a real-space anisotropic distortion of the magnetic order, whose structure encodes the symmetry of the underlying altermagnetic state. This impurity response offers a direct route to detecting altermagnetic order with locally resolved probes. We demonstrate this for both classical altermagnets, where vacancies generate anisotropic magnetization textures in a transverse magnetic field, and quantum models, where fluctuations induce longitudinal power-law decaying magnetic distortions even at zero field.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how vacancies in altermagnets create anisotropic magnetic distortions that reveal the symmetry of the altermagnetic state, detectable via local probes, with effects in both classical (transverse field) and quantum (zero-field fluctuations) regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand and identify the symmetry signatures of altermagnetic order through vacancy-induced magnetic textures, providing a direct detection method using locally resolved probes.
AI.method: Combination of microscopic simulations and low-energy field theory to analyze magnetic textures induced by vacancies in altermagnets, covering both classical and quantum models.
AI.result: Vacancies produce real-space anisotropic distortions encoding the altermagnetic symmetry; classical altermagnets show anisotropic magnetization textures under transverse field, while quantum models exhibit longitudinal power-law decaying distortions at zero field.
AI.conclusion: Vacancy-induced magnetic textures serve as a direct probe of altermagnetic order, with distinct signatures in classical and quantum altermagnets.

title: Second-harmonic signal in electric-field-modulated EPR spectra of Fe3 spin triangles
summary: We present electric-field-modulated electron paramagnetic resonance (EFM-EPR) measurements on centrosymmetric single crystals of the molecular spin triangle $\mathrm{[{Fe_3}O({O_2}CPh){_6}(py){_3}]ClO{_4}{\cdot}py}$ ($\bf{Fe_3}$). We provide the first observation of second harmonic EFM-EPR signal in polynuclear magnetic molecules. This signal is simulated and explained in terms of an electric-field induced modulation of the isotropic exchange in the molecule, and of their symmetry lowering resulting from a Jahn-Teller effect. Additionally, an unexpected first harmonic EFM-EPR signal is observed. Various plausible symmetry-breaking mechanisms are discussed in an attempt to explain this feature, whose observation is unexpected in a nominally centrosymmetric crystal.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first observation of second harmonic EFM-EPR signals in a molecular spin triangle (Fe₃), attributed to electric-field modulation of isotropic exchange and Jahn-Teller symmetry lowering, along with an unexpected first harmonic signal that challenges the centrosymmetric crystal assumption.
AI.motivation: To investigate electric-field effects on magnetic properties in polynuclear molecules and detect symmetry-breaking mechanisms via EFM-EPR.
AI.method: Electric-field-modulated electron paramagnetic resonance (EFM-EPR) measurements on centrosymmetric single crystals of [Fe₃O(O₂CPh)₆(py)₃]ClO₄·py.
AI.result: First observation of second harmonic EFM-EPR signal in polynuclear magnetic molecules; also observed an unexpected first harmonic signal.
AI.conclusion: The second harmonic signal arises from electric-field modulation of isotropic exchange and Jahn-Teller-induced symmetry lowering; the first harmonic signal suggests unidentified symmetry breaking in a nominally centrosymmetric crystal.

title: Fourier imaging of collective spontaneous emission modes in superradiant cold atomic clouds
summary: We measure the spatial pattern associated with the superradiant emission from a cloud of cold 87Rb atoms using Fourier imaging. We observe a highly directional, ring-shaped emission structure, which corresponds to a single collective jump operator associated to the most superradiant mode of the ensemble. Using spatial filtering, we isolate this channel and find the typical superradiant burst with superlinear scaling of the intensity with atom number. We compare our results to two models that describe the competition between the various decay channels, finding good agreement. Our work shows that the collective jump operators introduced by Carmichael et al. [Optics Communications 179, 417 (2000)] can be measured and manipulated.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the spatial pattern of superradiant emission from cold 87Rb atoms using Fourier imaging, observing a highly directional ring-shaped structure corresponding to the most superradiant collective mode. Spatial filtering isolates this channel, revealing superlinear intensity scaling with atom number, and results agree with models of competing decay channels.
AI.motivation: To experimentally measure and characterize the spatial structure of superradiant emission from cold atoms, specifically to identify and isolate the dominant collective jump operator predicted by Carmichael et al., and to demonstrate that these operators can be measured and manipulated.
AI.method: Fourier imaging of cold 87Rb atoms to measure spatial emission patterns, combined with spatial filtering to isolate the most superradiant collective decay channel.
AI.result: A highly directional, ring-shaped emission structure was observed, corresponding to a single collective jump operator. The isolated channel exhibited a superradiant burst with superlinear intensity scaling versus atom number. Experimental results showed good agreement with two theoretical models describing competition between decay channels.
AI.conclusion: Collective jump operators introduced by Carmichael et al. can be directly measured and manipulated, enabling control over superradiant emission channels in cold atomic ensembles.

title: Axion-Induced Casimir Interaction Between Graphene Plates
summary: Axion dark matter may induce observable electromagnetic effects in resonant cavity systems and potentially lead to modifications of the Casimir interaction. In this context, graphene represents an attractive platform owing to its tunable electromagnetic properties, and the fact that its electromagnetic response can be modelled microscopically from first principles within quantum field theory. The electromagnetic response induced by axion dark matter is investigated in a planar cavity consisting of parallel graphene interfaces in the presence of a homogeneous external magnetic field, incorporating finite temperature, chemical potential and dissipation through the graphene conductivity. Closed analytical expressions are obtained for the induced electric field and the resulting pressure. The pressure exhibits resonant enhancement at a series of plate separations satisfying $d_n=(2πn-φ(r))/m_a$, where $m_a$ is the axion mass and the phase $φ(r)$ is determined by the reflection coefficient $r$, which depends on the graphene conductivity evaluated at $ω=m_a$. The resonant structure is strongly influenced by the graphene chemical potential and damping parameter. In particular, increased doping, for example via a gate voltage, sharpens the resonances and amplifies the axion-induced signal. By comparing the resonantly enhanced signal with the conventional Casimir background, the parametric regimes in which the effect could become experimentally relevant are identified, with the strongest sensitivity obtained for highly doped low-dissipation graphene configurations operated near resonance. These results demonstrate that graphene-based Casimir-type configurations may provide a sensitive framework for probing axion-induced electromagnetic phenomena and highlight the interplay between axion electrodynamics, cavity resonances, and material properties in low-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates how axion dark matter induces electromagnetic effects in a planar cavity made of parallel graphene sheets under an external magnetic field. The axion-induced pressure exhibits resonant enhancement at specific plate separations determined by the axion mass, and the signal is significantly amplified by high doping and low dissipation in graphene, suggesting graphene-based Casimir cavities as sensitive probes for axion dark matter detection.
AI.motivation: To explore whether axion dark matter can produce detectable electromagnetic signals in graphene-based planar cavities, leveraging graphene's tunable electromagnetic properties and first-principles microscopic modeling within quantum field theory.
AI.method: The authors model the electromagnetic response of a planar cavity with parallel graphene interfaces in a homogeneous external magnetic field, incorporating finite temperature, chemical potential, and dissipation via the graphene conductivity. They derive closed-form analytical expressions for the induced electric field and pressure, and analyze resonant conditions where plate separation d_n = (2πn - φ(r))/m_a.
AI.result: The pressure shows resonant enhancement at specific separations linked to the axion mass. Increased graphene doping (e.g., via gate voltage) sharpens resonances and amplifies the axion-induced signal. The strongest sensitivity is predicted for highly doped, low-dissipation graphene configurations operated near resonance.
AI.conclusion: Graphene-based Casimir-type cavities may offer a sensitive experimental framework for detecting axion-induced electromagnetic phenomena, highlighting the interplay between axion electrodynamics, cavity resonances, and material properties in low-dimensional systems.

title: Parallel simulation of rarefied gas flows on unstructured meshes using the DIG-augmented DSMC method
summary: While the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) is a mainstream stochastic particle method for simulating rarefied gas flows, it incurs excessively high computational costs in the near continuum regime. As a hybrid acceleration approach coupling DSMC with macroscopic synthetic equations, the direct intermittent general synthetic iterative scheme (DIG) delivers fast convergence and asymptotic-preserving characteristics, which effectively alleviate the kinetic scale limitations inherent to standard DSMC. In this study, we develop a parallel DIG augmented DSMC solver for three dimensional rarefied gas flow simulations on unstructured meshes. On top of the standard DSMC algorithms for particle transport and collisions, a reliable intermittent coupling framework is constructed to exchange macroscopic flow data between the stochastic DSMC module and deterministic macroscopic synthetic equations. For parallel execution on unstructured grids, we employ a hybrid MPI architecture equipped with ghost cells to enable local particle tracking and batch inter-rank particle migration. A graph partitioning based dynamic load balancing strategy is also integrated to mitigate uneven particle distribution over computational domains. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solver achieves satisfactory agreement with the SPARTA DSMC. Leveraging the fast convergence and asymptotic-preserving properties of the DIG method, the required number of spatial cells and statistical sampling steps are drastically decreased, leading to substantial reductions in computational memory and runtime. This work presents an efficient high-performance numerical tool for high-fidelity simulations of rarefied flows over complex geometries. The code is available in the developer repository at the github link.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a parallel DIG-augmented DSMC solver for 3D rarefied gas flows on unstructured meshes, using hybrid MPI architecture with ghost cells, dynamic load balancing, and demonstrating substantial reductions in computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared to standard SPARTA DSMC.
AI.motivation: Standard DSMC incurs excessively high computational costs in the near-continuum regime due to kinetic scale limitations; hybrid acceleration approaches like DIG can alleviate these limitations but need to be extended to 3D unstructured meshes with parallel capabilities.
AI.method: A parallel DIG-augmented DSMC solver is developed with: (1) intermittent coupling framework exchanging macroscopic data between stochastic DSMC and deterministic macroscopic synthetic equations; (2) hybrid MPI architecture with ghost cells for local particle tracking and inter-rank migration; (3) graph partitioning based dynamic load balancing to mitigate uneven particle distribution.
AI.result: The solver achieves satisfactory agreement with SPARTA DSMC while drastically decreasing required spatial cells and statistical sampling steps, leading to substantial reductions in computational memory and runtime.
AI.conclusion: This work presents an efficient high-performance numerical tool for high-fidelity simulations of rarefied flows over complex geometries, with the code publicly available on GitHub.

title: Fluctuation theorems for autonomous work
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Published with Open Access on Dec. 12, 2025, in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (USA). This version contains the published article together with the published Supporting Information
summary: Classical fluctuation theorems for work have been obtained theoretically, and verified experimentally, within a non-autonomous framework in which work is performed on a system of interest, ${\cal S}$, by the external manipulation of a work parameter, such as a piston's position. Here we obtain fluctuation theorems within an autonomous framework in which ${\cal S}$ exchanges energy with a reversible work source, ${\cal R}$. The two subsystems, ${\cal R}$ and ${\cal S}$, interact with one another as they evolve under Hamiltonian or stochastic dynamics, without external intervention. In this setting, we must account for the back-action of ${\cal S}$ on ${\cal R}$, which is absent in the non-autonomous setting. We obtain autonomous versions of standard fluctuation theorems for work and entropy production. In each case, we argue, the autonomous fluctuation theorem reduces to its non-autonomous counterpart when ${\cal R}$'s inertia becomes infinitely large.

AI.tldr: This paper derives autonomous fluctuation theorems for work and entropy production, where a system S exchanges energy with a reversible work source R under Hamiltonian or stochastic dynamics without external intervention, showing they reduce to standard non-autonomous versions when R's inertia becomes infinite.
AI.motivation: Classical fluctuation theorems for work were derived in a non-autonomous framework with external manipulation of a work parameter. The authors aim to obtain fluctuation theorems within an autonomous framework where the system S interacts with a reversible work source R without external intervention, accounting for the back-action of S on R that is absent in non-autonomous settings.
AI.method: The authors consider an autonomous framework where two subsystems, R (reversible work source) and S (system of interest), interact with one another and evolve under Hamiltonian or stochastic dynamics without external intervention. They account for the back-action of S on R and derive autonomous versions of standard fluctuation theorems for work and entropy production.
AI.result: Autonomous versions of standard fluctuation theorems for work and entropy production are obtained. The autonomous fluctuation theorems reduce to their non-autonomous counterparts when R's inertia becomes infinitely large.
AI.conclusion: Fluctuation theorems can be extended to autonomous frameworks where the work source is part of the system, with the non-autonomous results recovered in the limit of infinite inertia of the work source.

title: Coherent vibrational wave packet motion in ErCry4a proteins monitors the redox state of the flavin chromophore
summary: Cryptochromes are blue-light-sensitive flavoproteins that play central roles in biological function. In European robin (Erithacus rubecula) ErCry4a proteins, optical excitation of their flavin chromophore forms a long-lived radical pair through a sequence of electron transfer steps across a tetradic chain of tryptophan residues, making them primary candidates for magnetoreception in night migratory songbirds. Recent quantum chemical calculations indicate that nonadiabatic couplings play a central role in the energy and charge transfer processes initiated by optical excitation. Here, we study these dynamics in ErCry4a using ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy with 10-fs time resolution in the 450-nm spectral range. We uncover a rapid, sub-50 fs red shift in stimulated emission, quenched within 360 fs by electron transfer from a nearby tryptophan moiety. While high-frequency excited state vibrations are rapidly damped, coherent motion involving several low-frequency vibrations persists during both the initial energy relaxation and the subsequent electron transfer. This is evidenced by probing the coherent vibrational motion of the formed FAD$^{\bullet-}$ radical anion and is independently validated by blocking the electron transfer through site-selective tryptophan mutation. Our results only provide insight into the role of nonadiabatic couplings for the initial steps of cryptochrome photoactivation and suggest a general strategy for redox-state-specific monitoring of charge transfer dynamics by probing coherent vibrational motion.

AI.tldr: Using ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy with 10-fs resolution, the authors study the photoactivation dynamics of the cryptochrome ErCry4a from the European robin, finding a sub-50 fs red shift in stimulated emission quenched within 360 fs by electron transfer, and observing persistent low-frequency coherent vibrations that serve as redox-state-specific probes of charge transfer.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of nonadiabatic couplings in the initial energy and charge transfer processes of cryptochrome photoactivation, which are central to theories of magnetoreception in night migratory songbirds.
AI.method: Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy with 10-fs time resolution in the 450-nm spectral range, combined with site-selective tryptophan mutation to block electron transfer and analysis of coherent vibrational motion.
AI.result: A rapid sub-50 fs red shift in stimulated emission was observed, quenched within 360 fs by electron transfer. High-frequency vibrations damp quickly, but low-frequency coherent vibrations persist through both energy relaxation and electron transfer, detectable via the FAD•− radical anion signal.
AI.conclusion: Nonadiabatic couplings are critical in the initial steps of cryptochrome photoactivation, and coherent vibrational motion offers a general strategy for redox-state-specific monitoring of charge transfer dynamics.

title: Large-scale first-principle simulations of amorphous indium oxide
summary: Amorphous indium oxide (a-In$_2$O$_3$) is a high-electron-mobility semiconductor of central importance in thin-film transistors and a promising photoanode for solar-driven water oxidation. Despite sustained experimental and computational investigations, the structural motifs underlying its unusual transport properties and the existence of O-O peroxide-like bonds within its network have remained unresolved. Here we develop a MACE-based machine-learned interatomic potential trained on first-principles molecular dynamics trajectories and use it to generate and analyze amorphous structures containing up to 5120 atoms, two orders of magnitude larger than those adopted in typical ab initio studies. We find X-ray structure factors in excellent quantitative agreement with experiment and we confirm that In$_2$O$_3$ is a poor glass former, with the likely presence of quasi-crystalline regions in amorphous samples. Our large-scale structural analysis reveals extended chains of edge-sharing InO$_k$ polyhedra providing a concrete structural basis for the high electron mobility of a-In$_2$O$_3$. Our results strongly support the formation of O-O peroxide-like bonds in the amorphous network, with a mean length of 1.5 Å. We show that these bonds introduce localized in-gap states near the conduction band minimum, acting as a source of intrinsic n-type self-doping and enhancing sub-gap optical absorption. These effects are detectable via a distinct Raman feature near 850 cm$^{-1}$ that is absent in the IR spectrum. Overall, our results establish a comprehensive structure-property picture of a-In$_2$O$_3$, provide directly testable experimental predictions, and suggest that controlled amorphization is a viable strategy for improving the photoelectrochemical activity of a-In$_2$O$_3$.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a MACE-based machine-learned interatomic potential to generate large-scale amorphous In₂O₃ structures, revealing edge-sharing InOₖ polyhedra chains as the basis for high electron mobility, confirming O-O peroxide-like bonds (~1.5 Å) that introduce in-gap states for intrinsic n-type doping and enhanced sub-gap absorption, with a distinct Raman signature at 850 cm⁻¹, establishing a comprehensive structure-property model with testable predictions.
AI.motivation: To resolve unresolved structural motifs (particularly O-O peroxide-like bonds) underlying the unusual transport properties of amorphous In₂O₃, which is critical for thin-film transistors and solar-driven water oxidation applications.
AI.method: A MACE-based machine-learned interatomic potential was trained on first-principles molecular dynamics trajectories and used to generate and analyze amorphous structures containing up to 5120 atoms—two orders of magnitude larger than typical ab initio studies.
AI.result: (1) X-ray structure factors show excellent quantitative agreement with experiment; (2) Confirmed poor glass-forming ability with quasi-crystalline regions; (3) Extended chains of edge-sharing InOₖ polyhedra explain high electron mobility; (4) O-O peroxide-like bonds (~1.5 Å) form in the amorphous network; (5) These bonds introduce localized in-gap states near the conduction band minimum, causing intrinsic n-type self-doping and enhanced sub-gap optical absorption; (6) A distinct Raman feature at 850 cm⁻¹ (absent in IR) is predicted as a detectable signature.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a comprehensive structure-property picture of a-In₂O₃, provides directly testable experimental predictions (Raman feature at 850 cm⁻¹), and suggests controlled amorphization is a viable strategy for improving its photoelectrochemical activity.

title: Bogolyubov excitons as a microscopic origin of two-level systems
summary: Two-level systems (TLS) are a leading source of decoherence and dielectric loss in Josephson-junction qubits, yet their microscopic origin remains unresolved. We propose an intrinsic, purely electronic TLS candidate: subgap bound states of Bogolyubov quasiparticles. We show that, in a model of a conventional superconductor with electron-electron attraction in the $s$-wave channel and repulsion in higher-angular-momentum channels, the latter produce an effective attraction between Bogolyubov quasiparticles, forming bound states. These Bogolyubov excitons resemble Bardasis--Schrieffer excitons but are driven by repulsive interactions. Bulk Bogolyubov excitons are not easily detectable through single-particle tunneling or other conventional probes, but we show that surface excitons couple to an external electric field and behave as two-level systems. We examine an idealized model of a bulk superconductor proximity-coupled to a two-dimensional repulsive metal, which could represent an external metallic or semiconductor layer or an underscreened region of the superconductor. The two levels correspond to the absence and presence of a single exciton, which carries an electric dipole moment and exhibits an avoided crossing with a resonator, as observed for TLS. Because this mechanism requires no defects and cannot be eliminated by screening or annealing, it suggests that TLS-like excitations may be intrinsic to superconductors.

AI.tldr: Subgap bound states of Bogolyubov quasiparticles (Bogolyubov excitons), formed by repulsive interactions in higher-angular-momentum channels, are proposed as an intrinsic, purely electronic source of two-level systems (TLS) that cause decoherence and dielectric loss in Josephson-junction qubits.
AI.motivation: Two-level systems (TLS) are a leading source of decoherence and dielectric loss in Josephson-junction qubits, yet their microscopic origin remains unresolved.
AI.method: The authors propose a model of a conventional superconductor with electron-electron attraction in the s-wave channel and repulsion in higher-angular-momentum channels, where the repulsion produces an effective attraction between Bogolyubov quasiparticles, forming bound states (Bogolyubov excitons). They examine an idealized model of a bulk superconductor proximity-coupled to a two-dimensional repulsive metal.
AI.result: Surface excitons couple to an external electric field and behave as two-level systems. The two levels correspond to the absence and presence of a single exciton, which carries an electric dipole moment and exhibits an avoided crossing with a resonator, as observed for TLS.
AI.conclusion: This mechanism requires no defects and cannot be eliminated by screening or annealing, suggesting that TLS-like excitations may be intrinsic to superconductors.

title: Design, Modeling, and Validation of Curvature-Based Shape-Aware Flexible Phased Arrays
summary: Knowledge of the shape of deformed, mechanically flexible phased arrays plays an important role in the ability to maintain their beam pattern. This work presents the design, modeling, and experimental validation of such arrays with integrated curvature-based shape sensing. We analyze, over a large set of representative deformed shapes, the sensor density required for effective deformation sensing under measurement noise; develop and experimentally validate a physical model relating measured strain to local board curvature; and demonstrate an end-to-end design of a shape-aware, 6-GHz, eight-element array in conformed and free-hanging scenarios, achieving an average reconstruction accuracy of ~6% while recovering beam-steering performance at radii of curvature below 3.6 cm. The system utilizes a low-cost, eight-channel, 360$^{\circ}$ digitally controlled phase-shifter platform useful for a wide range of smart-antenna experiments. The shape is recovered from low-rate surface measurements, independently of RF conditions and without feedback, making the approach a general sensing modality applicable beyond the beam correction demonstrated here.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a shape-aware, mechanically flexible phased array with integrated curvature-based shape sensing. Using low-rate surface strain measurements, the system reconstructs array deformation (~6% accuracy) and recovers beam-steering performance at radii <3.6 cm, demonstrated on a 6-GHz eight-element array with a low-cost 360° digital phase-shifter platform.
AI.motivation: Knowledge of deformed shape is critical for maintaining beam pattern in mechanically flexible phased arrays; existing methods lack independent, low-cost, feedback-free shape sensing.
AI.method: Analyzed sensor density requirements under noise; developed and validated a physical model relating strain to local board curvature; designed an end-to-end shape-aware 6-GHz eight-element array with integrated curvature sensing and a low-cost 8-channel 360° digitally controlled phase-shifter platform.
AI.result: Achieved average reconstruction accuracy of ~6% and recovered beam-steering performance at radii of curvature below 3.6 cm in conformed and free-hanging scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Shape recovery from low-rate surface measurements works independently of RF conditions and without feedback, making it a general sensing modality applicable beyond beam correction.

title: Electron-Phonon Functional Renormalization Group of Fermi Liquid Instabilities
summary: We formulate a functional renormalization group (FRG) ansatz for correlated electron models that incorporates electronic interactions as well as electron-phonon coupling (EPC) stemming from dispersive phonon bands. Particularizing to the RG flow of the electron-electron interaction vertex, we treat phonon- and electron-mediated Fermi liquid instabilities on equal footing as we analyze tentative electronic order parameters related to charge, spin, nematicity, and superconducting pairing. We illustrate the approach at the example of Peierls-type transitions we find for the Hubbard model on the square lattice coupled to acoustic phonon bands. Our method allows to incorporate full electronic and phononic ab initio input, and thus lends itself to the analysis of electronic order from intertwined electronic interactions and EPC at a microscopically most substantiated level.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a functional renormalization group (FRG) approach that treats electronic interactions and electron-phonon coupling (EPC) on equal footing to analyze competing Fermi liquid instabilities (charge, spin, nematicity, superconductivity). Applied to the Hubbard model with acoustic phonons on a square lattice, it captures Peierls-type transitions and allows incorporation of ab initio input.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat electronic interactions and electron-phonon coupling separately, preventing a unified analysis of competing order parameters in correlated electron systems where both mechanisms drive Fermi liquid instabilities.
AI.method: A functional renormalization group (FRG) ansatz is formulated that includes both electronic interactions and dispersive phonon-mediated coupling. The RG flow of the electron-electron interaction vertex is analyzed, treating phonon- and electron-mediated instabilities on equal footing.
AI.result: The method successfully captures Peierls-type transitions in the Hubbard model on a square lattice coupled to acoustic phonon bands, demonstrating the interplay between electronic correlations and EPC.
AI.conclusion: The FRG framework enables microscopically substantiated analysis of electronic order from intertwined electronic interactions and EPC, with full ab initio input possible for both electronic and phononic degrees of freedom.

title: Quantum Dot Moiré from Crossed MoS2 Nanoribbons
summary: Twisted atomically thin layers have attracted much attention for Moiré potential and correlated quantum phenomena. However, existing Moiré superlattices have largely been limited to extensive wavefunction without lateral confinement. Here we introduce a new platform where 1D nanoribbons of 2D MoS2 grown by vapor deposition can be easily superposed at various angles from stacking and transferring, to form Moiré quantum dots at their intersections with unique exciton physics. Angle-dependent Moiré intersections show enhanced exciton emission at commensurate angle 22 deg, which demonstrates faster relaxation at the cryogenic temperature. A size-dependent study further exhibits a reduced exciton energy and soften out-of-plane interlayer coupling for smaller Moiré areas. Our results reveal exciton physics turnability via precise overlapping of 1D nanoribbons.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new platform using 1D MoS2 nanoribbons stacked at various angles to form Moiré quantum dots at intersections, demonstrating enhanced exciton emission at a commensurate angle of 22°, faster cryogenic relaxation, and tunable exciton physics via size-dependent interlayer coupling.
AI.motivation: Existing Moiré superlattices are limited to extensive wavefunctions without lateral confinement; the authors aim to introduce a platform with confined Moiré quantum dots using 1D nanoribbons for tunable exciton physics.
AI.method: 1D MoS2 nanoribbons are grown by vapor deposition, then stacked and transferred at various angles to create Moiré quantum dots at intersections; angle-dependent and size-dependent optical characterization is performed.
AI.result: Enhanced exciton emission at a commensurate angle of 22°, faster relaxation at cryogenic temperatures, reduced exciton energy, and softened out-of-plane interlayer coupling for smaller Moiré areas.
AI.conclusion: Exciton physics can be tuned via precise overlapping of 1D nanoribbons, establishing a new platform for confined Moiré quantum dots.

title: Monte-Carlo solution of the Kondo model
summary: The Kondo model is a paradigmatic quantum impurity problem realized in a wide variety of experimental platforms and central to the study of strongly correlated electrons. We introduce a discrete model that exactly reproduces the multichannel Kondo model and demonstrate that it can be simulated efficiently. Using cluster Monte Carlo algorithms, we completely eliminate critical slowing down, providing direct access to universal crossover functions and transport properties across a broad range of parameters. Remarkably, the same model captures both the weak- and strong-coupling regimes, unifying descriptions traditionally derived in complementary limits and revealing their common origin. Our method naturally accommodates large channel numbers, anisotropy, interacting one-dimensional leads, and channel asymmetry, yielding predictions for transport properties in charge-Kondo devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a discrete model that exactly reproduces the multichannel Kondo model and can be simulated efficiently using cluster Monte Carlo algorithms, eliminating critical slowing down and providing direct access to universal crossover functions and transport properties across both weak- and strong-coupling regimes.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient simulation method for the multichannel Kondo model that overcomes computational limitations, particularly critical slowing down, and unifies descriptions of weak- and strong-coupling regimes.
AI.method: A discrete model exactly reproducing the multichannel Kondo model is introduced and simulated using cluster Monte Carlo algorithms, which eliminate critical slowing down and enable access to universal crossover functions.
AI.result: The method completely eliminates critical slowing down, provides direct access to universal crossover functions and transport properties across a broad parameter range, captures both weak- and strong-coupling regimes, and predicts transport properties in charge-Kondo devices.
AI.conclusion: The discrete model unifies traditionally complementary descriptions of the Kondo model, reveals their common origin, and naturally accommodates large channel numbers, anisotropy, interacting one-dimensional leads, and channel asymmetry.

title: Learned Committors as Reaction Coordinates for Nucleation Rates
summary: A central challenge in the analysis of first-order phase transitions is the identification of optimal reaction coordinates. In principle, the committor is the ideal choice; however, its computational cost has historically made it intractable. Here, we train a convolutional neural network ($p_B$-NN) as a proxy for the committor on brute-force committor labels and use it directly as the coordinate of a Markov state model. Applied to magnetisation reversal in the two-dimensional Ising model, $p_B$-NN reproduces brute-force nucleation rates across a range of thermodynamic conditions. The largest geometric cluster size also recovers accurate rates despite providing a poor pointwise predictor of the committor. These results demonstrate that an effective reaction coordinate for nucleation rate calculation must reliably separate the metastable and stable basins, but need not preserve the committor pointwise for every microstate. We stress that this distinction has direct implications for the choice of collective variable in rare-event simulations of nucleation more broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper trains a convolutional neural network (p_B-NN) as a proxy for the committor to compute nucleation rates in the 2D Ising model, showing that effective reaction coordinates need only separate metastable and stable basins rather than preserve the committor pointwise.
AI.motivation: Identifying optimal reaction coordinates (the committor) for first-order phase transitions is computationally intractable, motivating a more practical surrogate approach.
AI.method: A convolutional neural network (p_B-NN) is trained on brute-force committor labels and used as the coordinate in a Markov state model for nucleation rate calculations.
AI.result: p_B-NN reproduces brute-force nucleation rates across thermodynamic conditions; the largest geometric cluster size also yields accurate rates despite being a poor pointwise committor predictor.
AI.conclusion: An effective reaction coordinate must reliably separate metastable and stable basins but need not preserve the committor pointwise for every microstate, with implications for collective variable selection in rare-event simulations.

title: Equilibrium in a Reaction Network of Assemblies
summary: We study a mean-field reaction network whose species are assemblies built from identical atoms by reversible coagulation and fragmentation. Each assembly is an ordered binary tree, so the number of species of a given length grows combinatorially, as the Catalan numbers. The model nonetheless admits an explicit equilibrium and tractable stochastic dynamics. A finite volume $V$ sets a crossover length $l_c \sim \ln V$ that splits the equilibrium into two sectors. Below $l_c$ each assembly occurs in many copies and the rank-frequency distribution is Zipf-like; above $l_c$ individual species are rare and fluctuation-dominated. The statistical weight of the rare sector decays slowly with volume, controlling the finite-size scaling of diversity, Shannon entropy, and other assembly-weighted observables. The equilibrium also admits a transparent grand-canonical description in terms of a bond energy and an atomic chemical potential. Together these results make the model a controlled neutral baseline against which selection and driving in richer assembly networks can be measured.

AI.tldr: A mean-field reaction network of binary tree assemblies with reversible coagulation/fragmentation is studied. It has exact equilibrium, Catalan-number combinatorics, and exhibits a crossover length l_c ~ ln V splitting the system into a Zipf-like abundant sector and a fluctuation-dominated rare sector, with slow-decaying statistical weight controlling finite-size scaling of diversity and entropy.
AI.motivation: To construct a controlled, analytically tractable neutral baseline model for assembly reaction networks, against which selection and driving forces in more complex systems can be measured.
AI.method: Mean-field reaction network with species as ordered binary trees undergoing reversible coagulation and fragmentation; finite-volume analysis with grand-canonical description using bond energy and atomic chemical potential.
AI.result: The equilibrium exhibits a crossover length l_c ~ ln V separating a Zipf-like abundant sector (below l_c) from a rare, fluctuation-dominated sector (above l_c). The rare sector's statistical weight decays slowly with volume, controlling finite-size scaling of diversity and Shannon entropy.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a neutral baseline for studying selection and driving in richer assembly networks, with explicit equilibrium and tractable stochastic dynamics.

title: Reaction-network reasoning with frontier models for experimentally confirmed catalyst-selectivity hypotheses
summary: Catalysts are essential for sustainable chemical manufacturing, yet discovering novel architectures remains a bottleneck dominated by trial-and-error experimentation and computationally intensive screening. In complex reactions such as electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction, product selectivity is governed by dynamic interfacial, electrolyte, and potential factors as well as kinetic pathway competition. Conventional descriptor-based machine learning and computational potentials struggle to resolve these mechanistic branch points, primarily relying on static ground-state descriptors or bulk structural correlations rather than end-to-end topological pathway analysis. Here, we show that frontier language models, when strictly constrained to reason over explicit reaction networks, can discover novel catalysts by identifying the physical levers that govern pathway competition. We developed a human-AI co-thinking framework that enforces network invariance to extract testable hypotheses from complex chemical graphs. Applied to CO2 electroreduction, the framework identified ketene desorption and hydroxide capture as the acetate-forming pathway, and predicted a distinct adsorbed CO and CH2 coupling route to ketene. By isolating actionable control levers, specifically local alkalinity, controlled iron incorporation, and restricted interfacial proton-donor accessibility, the framework guided the prospective synthesis of a copper-iron oxide catalyst demonstrating a threefold increase in acetate selectivity over matched Cu-rich baselines. This mechanism-guided reasoning architecture shifts the computational paradigm from retrospective statistical prediction to forward-looking hypothesis generation, providing a broadly applicable blueprint for mechanism-guided materials discovery.

AI.tldr: Frontier language models constrained to reason over explicit reaction networks can discover novel catalysts by identifying physical levers that govern pathway competition, demonstrated by a human-AI co-thinking framework that predicted and experimentally validated a copper-iron oxide catalyst with threefold increased acetate selectivity in CO2 electroreduction.
AI.motivation: Catalyst discovery is bottlenecked by trial-and-error experimentation and computationally intensive screening; conventional descriptor-based ML and computational potentials rely on static ground-state descriptors rather than end-to-end topological pathway analysis, failing to resolve mechanistic branch points in complex reactions like CO2 electroreduction.
AI.method: A human-AI co-thinking framework that enforces network invariance by constraining frontier language models to reason over explicit reaction networks, extracting testable hypotheses from complex chemical graphs via topological pathway analysis.
AI.result: Identified ketene desorption and hydroxide capture as the acetate-forming pathway, predicted an adsorbed CO and CH2 coupling route to ketene, and isolated actionable control levers (local alkalinity, controlled iron incorporation, restricted interfacial proton-donor accessibility) that guided synthesis of a copper-iron oxide catalyst with threefold higher acetate selectivity.
AI.conclusion: This mechanism-guided reasoning architecture shifts the computational paradigm from retrospective statistical prediction to forward-looking hypothesis generation, providing a broadly applicable blueprint for mechanism-guided materials discovery.

title: Observation of giant nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching in superconductor-ferromagnet hybrids
summary: Magneto-thermal switch is a crucial thermal component which enables heat transfer control by the application of an external magnetic field. Recently, a nonvolatile behavior in magneto-thermal conductivity at zero magnetic field was observed in type-II and phase-separated superconductors owing to magnetic flux pinning nature, leading to an energy-efficient thermal control technology. However, the nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching ratio has been much lower than the volatile one in conventional materials. Here, we demonstrate a giant nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching in ferromagnetic Fe-superconducting Pb hybrids. The dispersion of pure Fe particles realizes increased electron and decreased phonon contributions in the thermal conductivity, which enhances the magneto-thermal switching ratio at the superconducting-to-normal conducting phase transition. Furthermore, in concert with trapped magnetic flux by supercurrent, ferromagnetic moment of Fe breaks the superconductivity of Pb matrix at zero magnetic field, enabling a significantly large nonvolatility even with a slight amount of Fe inclusions. Consequently, the nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching ratio reaches 719% in maximum at the Fe ratio of 8.7 vol%, which is more than twice the previous record value observed in Pb-Sn composites and the volatile one in pure Pb. This work broadens the exploration space and strategy for giant nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching materials.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a giant nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching effect in ferromagnetic Fe-superconducting Pb hybrids, achieving a record switching ratio of 719% at 8.7 vol% Fe, more than double previous records.
AI.motivation: Nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching enables energy-efficient thermal control, but previous nonvolatile switching ratios were much lower than volatile ones in conventional materials. The authors aimed to achieve a giant nonvolatile switching ratio.
AI.method: Fe particles were dispersed into a Pb superconducting matrix. The Fe dispersion increases electron thermal conductivity while decreasing phonon contributions. The ferromagnetic moment of Fe, combined with trapped magnetic flux from supercurrents, breaks superconductivity at zero magnetic field, enabling nonvolatility.
AI.result: A maximum nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching ratio of 719% was achieved at an Fe ratio of 8.7 vol%, more than twice the previous record in Pb-Sn composites and the volatile ratio in pure Pb.
AI.conclusion: This work broadens the exploration space and strategy for designing giant nonvolatile magneto-thermal switching materials by using ferromagnetic-superconducting hybrid systems.

title: Gate induced strain on a two-dimensional hole gas in silicon
summary: We show the effect of gate-induced strain on the valence band of a silicon (Si) metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) confined two-dimensional hole gas (2DHG). Increasing aluminum gate thickness, and thereby the strain in the channel, results in the onset of a second subband contributing to Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations. Temperature-dependent magnetotransport measurements reveal distinct cyclotron masses of $m_c^*=(0.36\pm0.04)m_0$ and $m_c^*=(0.49\pm0.02)m_0$. The measured cyclotron masses differ from those expected for an idealized heavy-hole (HH)/light-hole (LH) picture, reflecting the combined influence of quantum confinement, strain, and HH-LH mixing on the valence band.

AI.tldr: Gate-induced strain from aluminum gate thickness modifies the valence band of a Si MOS 2DHG, causing a second subband to appear in Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations, with measured cyclotron masses (0.36m₀ and 0.49m₀) deviating from ideal HH/LH expectations due to confinement, strain, and band mixing.
AI.motivation: To investigate how gate-induced strain affects the valence band structure of a silicon MOS-confined two-dimensional hole gas, particularly the emergence of higher subbands and deviation from idealized heavy-hole/light-hole behavior.
AI.method: Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations and temperature-dependent magnetotransport measurements were performed on Si MOS 2DHG samples with varying aluminum gate thickness to induce different strain levels.
AI.result: Increasing aluminum gate thickness (and thus strain) leads to a second subband contributing to oscillations; cyclotron masses measured as m_c*=(0.36±0.04)m₀ and m_c*=(0.49±0.02)m₀.
AI.conclusion: The observed cyclotron masses deviate from the ideal HH/LH picture, indicating that quantum confinement, strain, and HH-LH mixing collectively determine the valence band structure of Si 2DHGs.

title: Perturbations in the spin-orbital liquid (the Yao-Lee model)
summary: I investigate the stability of the spin-orbital liquid described by the Yao-Lee model in the presence of multiple perturbations that naturally arise in a recently proposed microscopic realization. While most perturbations are irrelevant and do not qualitatively alter the exact solvability, we find that the Kitaev interaction plays a special role: it couples to the $ \mathbb{Z}_2 $ gauge field and renders the visons mobile.

AI.tldr: The Yao-Lee model's spin-orbital liquid stability is studied under perturbations; most are irrelevant, but the Kitaev interaction couples to the ℤ₂ gauge field and mobilizes visons.
AI.motivation: To understand the stability of the spin-orbital liquid described by the Yao-Lee model under realistic perturbations arising from a microscopic realization.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of the Yao-Lee model perturbed by multiple perturbations, assessing their relevance and effect on exact solvability.
AI.result: Most perturbations are irrelevant, but the Kitaev interaction couples to the ℤ₂ gauge field and renders visons mobile.
AI.conclusion: The spin-orbital liquid is robust against most perturbations, except the Kitaev interaction which mobilizes visons, potentially altering the phase.

title: Bulk Boundary Condition for Surface Calculations in Density Functional Theory
summary: We present a bulk boundary condition formalism for surface calculations in Kohn--Sham density functional theory. The approach exploits the nearsightedness of electronic interactions in real space to restrict the calculation to a localized surface region. Within this region, the electron density is evaluated by leveraging the decay of the density matrix, with bulk values imposed on the density and electrostatic potential in the interior, and the electrostatic potential solved subject to bulk boundary conditions. The energy and atomic forces are computed using density-matrix-based expressions.
