Through representative calculations of surface and adsorption energies, we demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed formalism.

AI.tldr: Presents a bulk boundary condition formalism for surface calculations in Kohn-Sham DFT, leveraging nearsightedness to restrict calculations to a localized surface region and using density-matrix-based expressions for energy and forces.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate and efficient surface calculations in Kohn-Sham DFT by exploiting the nearsightedness of electronic interactions, avoiding full bulk+slab calculations.
AI.method: Restricts DFT calculations to a localized surface region using nearsightedness; evaluates electron density via decaying density matrix; imposes bulk values on density and electrostatic potential in the interior; solves electrostatic potential with bulk boundary conditions; computes energy and forces using density-matrix-based expressions.
AI.result: Demonstrates accuracy and efficiency through representative calculations of surface and adsorption energies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formalism is both accurate and efficient for surface calculations within Kohn-Sham DFT.

title: Repurposing acquisition devices into trigger-based timing synchronization of breakdown events during MITICA high voltage holding experiments
summary:
A critical requirement for MITICA -- a full-scale prototype of the heating Neutral Beam Injectors hosted at the Consorzio RFX Neutral Beam Test Facility for the ITER experiment -- is the capability to withstand a continuous voltage of 1MV across the vacuum gaps insulating the beam source from the grounded vessel. To validate such feature, a dedicated voltage-holding test campaign was conducted throughout 2024 and 2025 using a full-scale mock-up of the beam source. The tests also involved an accurate characterization of the associated breakdown events: vacuum dielectric failures which result in rapid potential drops and generate strong current discharges.
  This contribution will present a relative time reconstruction architecture based on cost-effective, embedded RedPitaya (Zynq-7000 FPGA) devices repurposed as timing hubs. These nodes function as configurable trigger multiplexers while simultaneously recording trigger signals as transients to facilitate the offline reconstruction of event sequences. The method allows self-calibration through measuring the static intrinsic delays of the optical fibers and internal logics, generating delay offsets to synchronize acquired waveforms across a sparse, connected-graph topology of both acquisition devices and hubs themselves.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a cost-effective, FPGA-based timing reconstruction system using RedPitaya devices for synchronizing breakdown event data across sparse networks during 1MV voltage-holding tests of MITICA's beam source mock-up.
AI.motivation: To validate MITICA's capability to withstand continuous 1MV voltage across vacuum gaps and to accurately characterize breakdown events (vacuum dielectric failures causing rapid potential drops and strong current discharges) during dedicated voltage-holding test campaigns conducted in 2024-2025.
AI.method: A relative time reconstruction architecture using cost-effective embedded RedPitaya (Zynq-7000 FPGA) devices configured as timing hubs. These nodes act as configurable trigger multiplexers while recording trigger signals as transients. Self-calibration is achieved by measuring static intrinsic delays of optical fibers and internal logics, generating delay offsets to synchronize waveforms across a sparse connected-graph topology of acquisition devices and hubs.
AI.result: A synchronization method enabling offline reconstruction of event sequences across a sparse, connected-graph topology of both acquisition devices and timing hubs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture enables accurate characterization of vacuum breakdown events in high-voltage test environments using affordable FPGA-based timing hubs with self-calibration capabilities.

title: Universality of Measurement-Induced Criticality under Symmetry-Breaking Measurements
summary: We study the critical properties of random quantum circuits with a $U(1)$ symmetry subject to local projective measurements that explicitly break this symmetry. We find that, at the measurement-induced phase transition, symmetry-breaking measurements act as a relevant perturbation at large scales, leading to the same universal critical properties as the corresponding monitored random circuit with non-symmetric unitary dynamics. In particular, we consider monitored $U(1)$-symmetric Haar-random circuits in the limit of large local Hilbert-space dimension, where the trajectory-averaged entanglement entropy can be exactly obtained in terms of a classical statistical mechanics model. In this model, the charge associated with the conservation law follows a symmetric simple exclusion process, in which symmetry-breaking measurements correspond to disordered defects that create and destroy charges. We prove that the charge correlation length remains finite for any measurement rate, ruling out a charge-sharpening transition, in contrast to the case of symmetry-preserving measurements. We further support our predictions at finite local Hilbert-space dimension through numerical finite-size scaling analyses of the entanglement transition in monitored $U(1)$-symmetric Haar and stabilizer random circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper studies $U(1)$-symmetric random quantum circuits under symmetry-breaking projective measurements, finding that such measurements act as a relevant perturbation driving the system to the same universal critical properties as non-symmetric monitored circuits. Using large local Hilbert-space dimension limits and classical statistical mechanics mapping, they show the charge follows a symmetric simple exclusion process with disordered defects, ruling out a charge-sharpening transition. Numerical simulations on Haar and stabilizer circuits support these findings.
AI.motivation: To understand how symmetry-breaking measurements affect measurement-induced phase transitions in $U(1)$-symmetric quantum circuits, specifically whether such measurements alter the universal critical properties or induce a charge-sharpening transition.
AI.method: The authors study monitored $U(1)$-symmetric Haar-random circuits in the large local Hilbert-space dimension limit, mapping the trajectory-averaged entanglement entropy to a classical statistical mechanics model. In this model, charge conservation follows a symmetric simple exclusion process, and symmetry-breaking measurements act as disordered defects. They also perform numerical finite-size scaling analyses on Haar and stabilizer random circuits at finite local Hilbert-space dimension.
AI.result: Symmetry-breaking measurements act as a relevant perturbation at large scales, leading to the same universal critical properties as monitored circuits with non-symmetric unitary dynamics. The charge correlation length remains finite for any measurement rate, ruling out a charge-sharpening transition (unlike symmetry-preserving measurements). Numerical results at finite dimension support these predictions.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-breaking measurements destroy the charge-sharpening transition and drive the system into the universality class of non-symmetric monitored random circuits, establishing that the nature of measurements (symmetry-breaking vs. symmetry-preserving) critically determines the phase diagram of monitored quantum circuits.

title: Generation and Characterization of Surface-Attached Ultrathin Liquid Sheets for Grazing-Incidence X-ray Scattering
summary: Capturing the ultrafast structural dynamics that occur at the solid-liquid interface is key to understanding adsorption, desorption, diffusion, and aggregation processes in catalysis and interfacial chemical reactions. Hard-X-ray scattering in grazing-incidence geometry can, in principle, access interfacial structural changes with angstrom-scale structural sensitivity and ultrafast temporal resolution. However, the long optical paths of the optical pump and hard-X-ray pulses inside the liquid sample pose significant challenges to the temporal resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and overall stability of such an experimental scheme. Here, we report a method for creating and characterizing ultrathin surface-attached free-flowing liquid sheets, whose submicrometer thickness enables ultrafast temporal resolution and reduces the bulk-liquid scattering contribution. The impinging-jet geometry produces stable micrometer-scale sheets whose morphology depends systematically on incidence angle, jet velocity, and capillary diameter. Gas-assisted shaping using a second capillary further narrows and thins the sheet, producing an extended ultrathin region and reducing the measured minimum thickness below 500~nm for acetonitrile. The resulting platform provides a reproducible, continuously flowing, surface-attached liquid geometry for grazing-incidence scattering experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a method to create ultrathin, surface-attached free-flowing liquid sheets (sub-500 nm thick for acetonitrile) using an impinging-jet geometry with gas-assisted shaping, enabling ultrafast temporal resolution and reduced bulk-liquid scattering for grazing-incidence hard-X-ray scattering studies of solid-liquid interfacial dynamics.
AI.motivation: Capturing ultrafast structural dynamics at the solid-liquid interface is key to understanding catalysis and interfacial chemical reactions, but existing hard-X-ray scattering schemes suffer from long optical paths in liquid samples, compromising temporal resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and stability.
AI.method: The method uses an impinging-jet geometry to produce stable micrometer-scale liquid sheets, with morphology systematically controlled by incidence angle, jet velocity, and capillary diameter. Gas-assisted shaping via a second capillary further narrows and thins the sheet, creating an extended ultrathin region.
AI.result: The technique produces reproducible, continuously flowing, surface-attached liquid sheets with measured minimum thickness below 500 nm for acetonitrile, reducing bulk-liquid scattering and enabling ultrafast temporal resolution.
AI.conclusion: This platform provides a viable liquid geometry for grazing-incidence scattering experiments, overcoming key limitations in temporal resolution and signal quality for studying ultrafast interfacial dynamics.

title: Signature in sound-mode of the exciton bilayer two-dimensional superfluid transition
summary: Obtaining definitive evidence of exciton superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers in zero magnetic field remains a major longstanding challenge since the condensate is electrically neutral, making its phase coherence difficult to detect directly. We show that the Anderson-Bogoliubov sound velocity provides a dynamical signature of exciton superfluidity. Across the BCS-BEC crossover, the velocity is known to discontinuously drop to zero at the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition. The magnitude of the drop has a strong density dependence. We compute this behavior, with the inclusion of finite-temperature screening, and determine the BKT transition using a renormalization-group approach. We further identify a temperature window which is experimentally accessible, where vortex-antivortex excitations strongly renormalize both the sound velocity and the transition temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that the Anderson-Bogoliubov sound velocity can serve as a dynamical signature of exciton superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers, showing a discontinuous drop at the BKT transition across the BCS-BEC crossover, with strong density and temperature dependence influenced by vortex-antivortex excitations and finite-temperature screening.
AI.motivation: To find a measurable dynamical signature of exciton superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers, which is notoriously difficult to detect directly due to the condensate's electrical neutrality and lack of phase coherence observability.
AI.method: The authors compute the Anderson-Bogoliubov sound velocity behavior across the BCS-BEC crossover, incorporate finite-temperature screening effects, and determine the BKT transition using a renormalization-group approach.
AI.result: The sound velocity discontinuously drops to zero at the BKT transition, with the drop magnitude showing strong density dependence. A temperature window exists where vortex-antivortex excitations significantly renormalize both the sound velocity and transition temperature.
AI.conclusion: The Anderson-Bogoliubov sound velocity provides an experimentally accessible dynamical signature for detecting exciton superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers at zero magnetic field.

title: Interfacial chirality-induced magnetic-field-free switching with high energy efficiency in all-vdW heterostructures
comment: Accepted by Nature Communications; 30 pages; 4 main figures; 12 supporting figures
summary: Chirality, a central concept across many scientific disciplines, continues to inspire the discovery of novel physical phenomena. In condensed matter physics, structural chirality - defined by the absence of mirror plane symmetries - has primarily been explored in bulk materials. However, new chiral phenomena can emerge uniquely at the interface, distinct from their bulk counterparts, when a chiral material forms a heterostructure. Here, we demonstrate that all van-der-Waals (vdW) heterostructure composed of the chiral Co1/3TaS2 and the achiral vdW ferromagnet Fe3GeTe2 exhibits two distinct and unconventional spin-orbit torques originating from the interfacial chirality. These torques enable magnetic-field-free switching of perpendicular magnetization with ultralow current density ~ 10^6 A/cm^2 and minimal power dissipation < 10^15 W/m^3. Moreover, by replacing Fe3GeTe2 with a similar vdW ferromagnet, Fe3GaTe2, but of higher Curie temperature, we achieved the magnetic-field-free switching at room temperature in the Fe3GaTe2/Co1/3TaS2 vdW heterostructure. Our findings establish interfacial chirality as a powerful new handle for spintronic control, opening a new pathway to explore chirality-induced phenomena beyond the bulk symmetry constraints - and paving the way toward highly efficient, low-power spintronic devices based on all-vdW heterostructures.

AI.tldr: Interfacial chirality in all-van-der-Waals heterostructures (chiral Co1/3TaS2 + achiral ferromagnet Fe3GeTe2 or Fe3GaTe2) generates two unconventional spin-orbit torques, enabling magnetic-field-free switching of perpendicular magnetization at ultralow current density (~10^6 A/cm²) and minimal power dissipation (<10¹⁵ W/m³), with room-temperature operation achieved via Fe3GaTe2.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that interfacial chirality, as distinct from bulk structural chirality, can generate novel spintronic phenomena (unconventional spin-orbit torques) in van-der-Waals heterostructures, enabling energy-efficient, field-free magnetization switching.
AI.method: All-vdW heterostructures were fabricated by combining chiral Co1/3TaS2 with achiral vdW ferromagnets (Fe3GeTe2 or Fe3GaTe2). Spin-orbit torque measurements and magnetization switching experiments were performed, with material selection (Fe3GaTe2) to achieve room-temperature operation via its higher Curie temperature.
AI.result: Two distinct unconventional spin-orbit torques arise from interfacial chirality; magnetic-field-free switching of perpendicular magnetization is achieved at ultralow current density ~10⁶ A/cm² and minimal power dissipation <10¹⁵ W/m³; room-temperature switching is realized in Fe3GaTe2/Co1/3TaS2.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial chirality provides a new mechanism for spintronic control beyond bulk symmetry constraints, enabling highly efficient, low-power spintronic devices based on all-vdW heterostructures.

title: Tunable Emergent Gauge Fields from Skyrmions in a Quasicrystalline Lattice
summary: We study magnetic skyrmions in a two-dimensional quasicrystalline lattice using a classical Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions and an external magnetic field. The competition between the skyrmion-skyrmion repulsion and an emergent quasiperiodic pinning landscape gives rise to a sequence of distinct skyrmion lattice configurations as a function of field. The resulting hierarchy of quasiperiodic pinning potentials, characterized by closely spaced quasi-degenerate minima, enables a quasi-continuous suppression of the skyrmion density as the saturation field is approached, in sharp contrast to the strongly first-order collapse of skyrmion crystals on periodic lattices. This provides a direct mechanism for controlling the topological charge and, consequently, the emergent gauge field for itinerant electrons. As a consequence, the Hall conductivity can be strongly modified with small changes in the magnetic field and driven smoothly to zero near saturation. This field-controlled tunability, rooted in the underlying multistability, identifies quasicrystalline magnets as a platform for tunable topological textures, with potential applications in magnetic memory and magnetoelectronic response.

AI.tldr: Magnetic skyrmions on a quasicrystalline lattice exhibit quasi-continuous density suppression under magnetic field due to quasiperiodic pinning, enabling smooth tuning of topological charge and Hall conductivity, unlike the first-order collapse on periodic lattices.
AI.motivation: To understand how quasicrystalline order, with its hierarchical pinning landscape, modifies the behavior of magnetic skyrmions compared to conventional periodic lattices, and to explore its potential for controlling topological textures.
AI.method: Classical Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions and external magnetic field on a two-dimensional quasicrystalline lattice; analysis of skyrmion configurations as a function of field strength.
AI.result: Quasiperiodic pinning yields closely spaced quasi-degenerate minima, enabling quasi-continuous skyrmion density suppression near saturation, contrasting with first-order collapse on periodic lattices; Hall conductivity can be smoothly driven to zero with small field changes.
AI.conclusion: Quasicrystalline magnets provide a platform for tunable topological textures via field control, with implications for magnetic memory and magnetoelectronic devices.

title: Interplay of Quasiperiodic Criticality and the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect
summary: Quasiperiodic lattices can host critical eigenstates, whereas nonreciprocal hopping in non-Hermitian lattices can induce non-Hermitian skin effect. In this work, we investigate localization phenomena in a Hatano--Nelson model with quasiperiodically modulated hopping amplitudes, where nonreciprocity arises from unequal modulation strengths of the right and left hoppings. Using a non-unitary gauge transformation, we map the non-Hermitian system into a Hermitian quasiperiodic system and obtain an exact analytical expression for the Lyapunov exponent in the thermodynamic limit. Under periodic boundary conditions, inverse participation ratios and finite-size scaling analysis are used to identify the quasiperiodic critical regimes. The comparison shows that parameter regimes hosting quasiperiodic critical states under periodic boundary conditions can exhibit the non-Hermitian skin effect under open boundary conditions. Furthermore, the non-Hermitian skin effect associated with quasiperiodic critical regimes is also observed in representative long-range hopping models and multiband extensions. Our results provide an analytically controlled perspective on how quasiperiodicity, modulated nonreciprocity, and boundary conditions jointly shape the non-Hermitian skin effect in critical regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates localization in a non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model with quasiperiodically modulated hopping, revealing that quasiperiodic critical regimes under periodic boundary conditions can exhibit the non-Hermitian skin effect under open boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: To understand how quasiperiodicity, modulated nonreciprocity, and boundary conditions jointly shape the non-Hermitian skin effect in critical regimes.
AI.method: Non-unitary gauge transformation maps the non-Hermitian system to a Hermitian quasiperiodic system; Lyapunov exponent derived analytically in thermodynamic limit; inverse participation ratios and finite-size scaling analysis used under periodic boundary conditions.
AI.result: Parameter regimes hosting quasiperiodic critical states under periodic boundary conditions can exhibit the non-Hermitian skin effect under open boundary conditions. This effect also appears in long-range hopping models and multiband extensions.
AI.conclusion: The interplay of quasiperiodicity, nonreciprocity, and boundary conditions provides an analytically controlled perspective on the non-Hermitian skin effect in critical regimes.

title: Charge-partition pathways in strong-field photoionization of carbonyl sulfide monomers and dimers
summary: Strong-field photoionization of molecules and molecular clusters gives rise to a rich variety of fragmentation pathways governed by charge localization and redistribution on ultrafast timescales. Here, we report a velocity-map imaging study of the strong-field photoionization and fragmentation of carbonyl sulfide (OCS) monomers and dimers driven by 150 femtosecond (fs) laser pulses at 775~nm. The images of the total kinetic-energy and angular distributions of the OCS$^{2+}$, S$^+$, and CO$^+$ fragments were interpreted with the help of electronic-structure calculations of the potential energy surfaces for OCS$^+$ and OCS$^{2+}$. We identify distinct dissociation pathways of singly and doubly ionized OCS, including two-body breakup channels of OCS$^+$ into $\mathrm{S}^+ + \mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{CO}^+ + \mathrm{S}$, dissociation of OCS$^{2+}$ into $\mathrm{S}^+ + \mathrm{CO}$$^+$ as well as higher-order three-body fragmentation. In addition, the images of the OCS$^{2+}$ channel exhibit near-zero-momentum components, low-energy isotropic features, and highly anisotropic contributions at high kinetic energies that cannot be explained by monomer ionization alone. Analysis of the KER distributions and angular anisotropies indicates that these features originate from the breakup of multiply charged OCS dimers ((OCS)$_2^{2+}$, (OCS)$_2^{3+}$, and (OCS)$_2^{4+}$) through charge-separation channels. Our results illustrate how dynamic signatures of strong-field fragmentation evolve from intramolecular dissociation in isolated molecules to intermolecular charge separation in weakly bound clusters providing a unified picture of charge-driven dissociation dynamics beyond the single-molecule limit.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates strong-field photoionization and fragmentation of OCS monomers and dimers using velocity-map imaging with 150 fs laser pulses at 775 nm. By combining experimental KER and angular distributions with electronic-structure calculations, the authors identify distinct dissociation pathways for singly and doubly charged OCS monomers, and attribute anomalous low-energy isotropic and high-energy anisotropic features to charge-separation channels from multiply charged OCS dimers ((OCS)₂²⁺, (OCS)₂³⁺, (OCS)₂⁴⁺), revealing a transition from intramolecular dissociation to intermolecular charge separation.
AI.motivation: To understand how charge localization and redistribution on ultrafast timescales govern fragmentation pathways in strong-field ionization, and to bridge the gap between intramolecular dissociation dynamics in isolated molecules and intermolecular charge-separation dynamics in weakly bound clusters.
AI.method: Velocity-map imaging (VMI) of OCS monomers and dimers ionized by 150 fs, 775 nm laser pulses, combined with electronic-structure calculations of potential energy surfaces for OCS⁺ and OCS²⁺. Kinetic-energy release (KER) and angular distribution analyses were performed.
AI.result: Identified two-body breakup channels of OCS⁺ (S⁺+CO, CO⁺+S), dissociation of OCS²⁺ (S⁺+CO⁺), and three-body fragmentation. OCS²⁺ images show near-zero-momentum, low-energy isotropic, and high-energy anisotropic components originating from multiply charged dimer breakup.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic signatures of strong-field fragmentation evolve from intramolecular dissociation in isolated molecules to intermolecular charge separation in weakly bound clusters, providing a unified picture of charge-driven dissociation dynamics beyond the single-molecule limit.

title: Theoretical exploration of Be Ag(II) F phases and their magnetic properties using learning algorithms
comment: 8 pages, 4 Figures, 2 Tables, and electronic supplement of 18 pages
summary: The search for novel silver(II) fluorides is driven by their potential as electronic and magnetic analogues to high temperature cuprate(II) superconductor precursors. Here, we explore the previously uncharted Be Ag(II) F chemical space using global structure prediction algorithms combined with first principles calculations. Focusing on the AgBeF4 stoichiometry, we identify the five lowest enthalpy polymorphs crystallizing in the C2, P minus 1, and P 21/c space groups. All polymorphs show an antiferromagnetic ground state, with AgBeF4_4 and AgBeF4_5 exhibiting unprecedented strong superexchange interactions of J equal circa to minus 460meV and J equal circa to minus 359meV respectively. Those high J values are due to the presence of either [Ag2F7] for AgBeF4_4, or related infinite [AgF2/2+2/1]2 minus chains for AgBeF4_5. Although the phases are found to be metastable with respect to binary difluorides, the thermodynamic analysis suggests that they could be targeted via synthetic routes employing fluorine radicals, with reaction enthalpies reaching minus 370 kJ/mol.

AI.tldr: Using global structure prediction and first-principles calculations, the study explores the AgBeF4 stoichiometry in the Be-Ag(II)-F chemical space, identifying five low-enthalpy antiferromagnetic polymorphs (C2, P-1, P21/c space groups). Two polymorphs show strong superexchange interactions (J ≈ -460 meV, -359 meV) due to [Ag2F7] or [AgF2/2+2/1]2- chains. Though metastable, synthesis via fluorine radicals is thermodynamically feasible.
AI.motivation: To search for novel silver(II) fluorides as potential electronic and magnetic analogues to high-temperature cuprate(II) superconductor precursors.
AI.method: Global structure prediction algorithms combined with first-principles calculations to explore the Be-Ag(II)-F chemical space at the AgBeF4 stoichiometry.
AI.result: Five low-enthalpy polymorphs identified (C2, P-1, P21/c space groups), all antiferromagnetic. AgBeF4_4 and AgBeF4_5 show strong superexchange interactions (J ≈ -460 meV and -359 meV) due to [Ag2F7] and infinite [AgF2/2+2/1]2- chains, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The phases are metastable relative to binary difluorides but thermodynamically accessible via fluorine radical synthetic routes, with reaction enthalpies up to -370 kJ/mol.

title: Polycrystalline ferroelectric croconic acid for multisource environmental energy harvesting
summary: The development of organic ferroelectric materials through scalable and simplified fabrication routes remains a major challenge for next-generation energy-harvesting technologies. Here, polycrystalline croconic acid (CA) thin films are fabricated by vacuum sublimation onto Ar plasma-treated flexible substrates and stabilized by in situ encapsulation with an adamantane-based remote plasma polymer. This solvent-free strategy effectively suppresses surface degradation under ambient conditions, providing long-term stability. Piezoresponse force microscopy confirms robust ferroelectricity with an oblique polarization orientation, well-defined domains, and low nanoscale coercive fields. The films were integrated into multilayer piezoelectric and pyroelectric devices. The piezoelectric performance strongly depends on film thickness, while embedding the CA layer between dielectric polymeric films significantly improves the macroscopic response, reaching power densities of up to 37 microW m-2 for ca. 2 micrometer CA films. Despite the common assumption that high crystallinity is required to sustain ferro-, piezo-, and pyroelectricity, these polycrystalline CA films exhibit remarkable RT pyroelectricity, a property not previously demonstrated in CA-based devices. A pyroelectric coefficient of ca. 10 microC m-2 K-1 highlights a functional response comparable to that of well-established organic and inorganic pyroelectric materials, demonstrating the potential of CA thin films for thermal energy harvesting. Beyond their functional performance, the proposed low-T fabrication route combines deposition and encapsulation in a single in situ process, simplifying device fabrication. Its compatibility with scalable vacuum technologies, flexible substrates, and further process optimization makes this approach highly promising for developing low-cost, lead-free, multisource energy-harvesting systems.

AI.tldr: Polycrystalline croconic acid thin films fabricated via vacuum sublimation on plasma-treated flexible substrates with in situ encapsulation exhibit robust ferroelectricity, piezoelectricity with power densities up to 37 μW m⁻², and previously unreported room-temperature pyroelectricity (coefficient ~10 μC m⁻² K⁻¹), enabled by a solvent-free, scalable fabrication route.
AI.motivation: Developing organic ferroelectric materials through scalable, simplified, and solvent-free fabrication routes remains a major challenge for next-generation, flexible, and lead-free energy-harvesting technologies.
AI.method: Polycrystalline croconic acid (CA) thin films were fabricated by vacuum sublimation onto Ar plasma-treated flexible substrates, followed by in situ encapsulation with an adamantane-based remote plasma polymer. Films were characterized by piezoresponse force microscopy and integrated into multilayer piezoelectric/pyroelectric devices.
AI.result: CA films showed robust ferroelectricity with oblique polarization and low nanoscale coercive fields. Piezoelectric power density reached 37 μW m⁻² for ~2 μm CA films. Room-temperature pyroelectric coefficient of ~10 μC m⁻² K⁻¹ was demonstrated, comparable to established organic and inorganic pyroelectrics.
AI.conclusion: The solvent-free, low-temperature fabrication route combining deposition and encapsulation in a single in situ process is compatible with scalable vacuum technologies and flexible substrates, making it highly promising for low-cost, lead-free, multisource energy-harvesting systems.

title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Electron-Phonon Systems via Non-Gaussian Matrix Product States
summary: We investigate strongly correlated electron-phonon (e-ph) systems via a non-Gaussian matrix product state method. By combining non-Gaussian states with matrix product states, our method efficiently characterizes the intractable entanglement between strongly correlated electrons and phononic modes of unbounded Hilbert space, enabling scalable simulations across broad parameter regimes. In one-dimensional generalized Hubbard--Holstein (HH) models, we identify a pronounced tendency toward phase separation (PS), an instability relevant to recent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy observations on doped cuprate chain. In two-dimensional HH models, we construct the phase diagram at half-filling featuring a metallic phase emerging from the competition between non-local phonon-mediated attraction and local Hubbard repulsion. Upon doping, we elucidate the role of soft phonons in stabilizing stripe phases. In the antiferromagnet, the stabilization of the fully filled stripe is attributed to a local retardation effect, wherein the charge order is pinned by phonons, leading to a diminished response to spin fluctuations. In the doped charge-density-wave regime, a novel bipolaronic stripe phase with an enlarged unit cell is stabilized via a non-local retardation effect, where long-range phonon-mediated interactions suppress PS. Our work establishes a systematic route to decoding the e-ph interplay that is crucial for superconductivity.

AI.tldr: A non-Gaussian matrix product state method is developed to simulate strongly correlated electron-phonon systems, revealing phase separation, metallic phases, and novel bipolaronic stripe phases in Hubbard-Holstein models across 1D and 2D regimes.
AI.motivation: To overcome the computational challenge of simulating strongly correlated electron-phonon systems where phononic modes have unbounded Hilbert space and exhibit intractable entanglement with electrons.
AI.method: Non-Gaussian matrix product state method combining non-Gaussian states with matrix product states for efficient characterization of electron-phonon entanglement in unbounded Hilbert spaces.
AI.result: 1D generalized Hubbard-Holstein models show pronounced phase separation tendency relevant to ARPES observations on doped cuprate chains. 2D models at half-filling reveal a metallic phase from competition between non-local phonon-mediated attraction and local Hubbard repulsion. Upon doping, soft phonons stabilize stripe phases, including a novel bipolaronic stripe phase with enlarged unit cell via non-local retardation effects.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a systematic route to decoding electron-phonon interplay crucial for superconductivity.

title: Helically Enhanced Chiroptical Response and Symmetry Breaking in Conjugated Polymers
summary: Chiral $π$-conjugated polymers are an attractive material platform for spin polarized carrier-transport and spectroscopy, but fundamental considerations for how torsional disorder influences the response properties of the material have not been considered. Here we combine atomistic electronic structure modeling with with experimental spectroscopic measurements to examine symmetry breaking in the prototypical $π$-conjugated polymer polyacetylene, (CH)$_x$. Chiral (CH)$_x$ oligomers are generated in distinct conformations which differ in their out-of-plane tonsorial ordering. We find that a \textit{helical }conformation introduces orders of magnitude enhanced chiroptical activity due to a solenoid effect. This effect is visualized by the Transition Chiral Tensor analysis which shows signatures of domain ordering which eliminates destructive interference between electric and magnetic contributions. These findings highlight the capability to develop a hierarchical interpretation relating local, fragment symmetry breaking to global, nonlocal interactions governing chiroptical response in emerging chiral materials.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that helical ordering in chiral π-conjugated polymers like polyacetylene dramatically enhances chiroptical activity via a solenoid effect, explained by transition chiral tensor analysis revealing domain ordering that eliminates destructive interference between electric and magnetic contributions.
AI.motivation: To understand how torsional disorder and chiral conformation influence the chiroptical response properties of π-conjugated polymers, which had not been previously considered despite their importance for spin-polarized transport and spectroscopy.
AI.method: Combined atomistic electronic structure modeling with experimental spectroscopic measurements on polyacetylene (CH)ₓ oligomers in distinct conformations differing in out-of-plane torsional ordering, analyzed using Transition Chiral Tensor analysis.
AI.result: Helical conformation introduces orders of magnitude enhanced chiroptical activity due to a solenoid effect; domain ordering signatures eliminate destructive interference between electric and magnetic contributions.
AI.conclusion: The findings enable a hierarchical interpretation linking local fragment symmetry breaking to global nonlocal interactions governing chiroptical response in chiral materials.

title: Anomalous Reflection of Caustic Spin-Wave Beams in a Magnonic Waveguide
summary: Reflection of waves at interfaces is conventionally governed by Snell's law, which follows from conservation of momentum parallel to the interface. Here we show experimentally that caustic spin-wave beams in anisotropic media obey a fundamentally different reflection mechanism. Applying time-resolved Kerr microscopy to a yttrium iron garnet waveguide, we observe that reflected beams are selected by transitions between caustic points on the anisotropic iso-frequency contour rather than by momentum conservation. As a consequence, the reflected carrier wave vector and wavefront orientation exhibit trends opposite to those predicted by Snell's law. By tuning the magnitude and orientation of an external magnetic field, we continuously control the resulting reflection process and beam routing. Our results establish caustic-point transitions as a distinct reflection law for anisotropic wave beams and provide a route towards reconfigurable magnonic beam steering.

AI.tldr: Spin-wave beams in anisotropic media reflect via caustic-point transitions on the iso-frequency contour, not by Snell's law, allowing reconfigurable magnonic beam steering.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that wave reflection in anisotropic media can deviate fundamentally from Snell's law, specifically for caustic spin-wave beams.
AI.method: Time-resolved Kerr microscopy on a yttrium iron garnet waveguide, with external magnetic field tuning to control reflection.
AI.result: Reflected beams are selected by transitions between caustic points on the anisotropic iso-frequency contour; carrier wave vector and wavefront orientation show opposite trends to Snell's law.
AI.conclusion: Caustic-point transitions establish a new reflection law for anisotropic wave beams, enabling reconfigurable magnonic beam steering.

title: Bond, orbital and spin order in d4/d6/d7 perovskite oxides: successes and limitations of foundation interatomic potentials
summary: Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are rapidly replacing density-functional theory (DFT) for modeling structure and nuclear dynamics, making their fidelity in strongly correlated systems an urgent question. We test three foundation potentials on the low-temperature order of three correlated, isostructural ABO3 perovskite oxides: LaMnO3 (d4), LaCoO3 (d6), and NdNiO3 (d7). We run molecular dynamics for 1 ns on 80- and 160-atom supercells from 50 to 300 K with no system-specific training. These oxides expose three distinct classes of low-temperature order that define a hierarchy of difficulty for the potentials. The scalar class, represented by NdNiO3, has a simple geometric fingerprint and is captured. The vector class, represented by LaMnO3, requires identifying which Cartesian axis carries the long bond at each site, and is captured in magnitude but not in symmetry. The on-site class, represented by the low-spin to high-spin crossover in LaCoO3, is a purely local multiplet population shift with no spatial order parameter and remains inaccessible to present-day MLIPs.

AI.tldr: Three foundation MLIPs are tested on low-temperature ordered phases of LaMnO3, LaCoO3, and NdNiO3. They capture scalar order (NdNiO3), partially capture vector order (LaMnO3) with wrong symmetry, and fail entirely on on-site multiplet order (LaCoO3).
AI.motivation: Foundation MLIPs are replacing DFT for modeling structure and dynamics, but their fidelity in strongly correlated systems is unknown. This work tests them on correlated perovskite oxides with diverse low-temperature orders.
AI.method: Three foundation potentials are used to run 1 ns molecular dynamics on 80- and 160-atom supercells of LaMnO3, LaCoO3, and NdNiO3 from 50 to 300 K without system-specific training.
AI.result: NdNiO3 (scalar class) is captured; LaMnO3 (vector class) captures magnitude but wrong symmetry; LaCoO3 (on-site class, spin-crossover) is inaccessible to current MLIPs.
AI.conclusion: Current foundation MLIPs fail for strongly correlated systems with local multiplet (on-site) order, partially succeed for vector order, and capture scalar order, revealing a hierarchy of difficulty.

title: State-Averaged Density Matrix Embedding Theory for Local Excitations
summary: Density matrix embedding theory (DMET) provides an elegant framework in quantum chemistry to describe local properties of chemical systems that allows a high-level method being used to solve an embedded subsystem constructed based on a low-level treatment of the whole system, and therefore achieves a balance between efficiency and accuracy. However, because the embedded subspace in DMET is typically constructed from the mean-field ground state Slater determinant, the resulting bath orbitals inherently favor the ground state, leading to unbalanced descriptions of ground and excited states for local excitations. In this work, we first demonstrate the starting-point dependence of DMET in excitation energy calculations, and then generalize original ground-state based DMET by extending the starting point from the single Slater determinant to state-averaged (SA) complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF), hence termed as SA-DMDT. In calculations of magnetic anisotropy and excitation energies of transition metal and lanthanide complexes, SA-DMET shows significant improvement in accuracy compared to the single-state DMET. Configuration-averaged Hartree-Fock (CAHF), which is equivalent to SA-CASSCF when all states in the chosen active space are equally averaged, is found to give comparable accuracy as a DMET starting point, thus offering a more efficient choice for state-averaged embedding. Finally, the recently proposed non-orthongal atomic-orbital-based DMET (AO-DMET) is tested on various systems and gives very promising results in all cases. These results establish SA-DMET, especially in combination with AO-DMET and CAHF, as a robust and efficient embedding framework for local excited states in strongly correlated metal complexes.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes density matrix embedding theory (DMET) from ground-state to state-averaged (SA) formulations using SA-CASSCF or CAHF starting points, significantly improving accuracy for local excited states and magnetic anisotropy in transition metal and lanthanide complexes. The combination with AO-DMET and CAHF is established as a robust embedding framework.
AI.motivation: Standard DMET constructs embedded subspaces from a ground-state mean-field Slater determinant, which biases bath orbitals toward the ground state and leads to unbalanced descriptions of ground and excited states for local excitations. This work aims to overcome this starting-point dependence in excitation energy calculations.
AI.method: The authors generalize ground-state DMET by replacing the single Slater determinant starting point with state-averaged (SA) complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF), termed SA-DMET. They also test configuration-averaged Hartree-Fock (CAHF) as a more efficient alternative, and evaluate non-orthogonal atomic-orbital-based DMET (AO-DMET) on various systems.
AI.result: SA-DMET shows significant improvement in accuracy over single-state DMET for magnetic anisotropy and excitation energies of transition metal and lanthanide complexes. CAHF yields comparable accuracy to SA-CASSCF as a DMET starting point. AO-DMET gives very promising results across all tested systems.
AI.conclusion: SA-DMET, especially when combined with AO-DMET and CAHF, provides a robust and efficient embedding framework for treating local excited states in strongly correlated metal complexes.

title: Influence of electronic correlations on disorder-induced loop currents in high-Tc superconductors
summary: Time-reversal symmetry breaking in superconducting systems can manifest itself in the form of currents which are induced by inhomogeneities in the charge and order parameter distribution. With regard to cuprates such states have been theoretically studied in the overdoped region of the phase diagram where the inhomogeneities are related to out-of plane dopants. In this paper we will extend previous work by including local correlations within the unrestricted Gutzwiller approximation in order to study its impact on the induced loop currents. In addition, we investigate the effect of next-nearest neighbor hopping which extends the TRSB phase towards half-filling. We find that in general correlations lead to a suppression of loop currents, however, the Gutzwiller approach can sustain such states to larger values of the local on-site repulsion as compared to the Hartree-Fock approximation. Our investigations allow for an estimation of the local magnetic moment emerging from impurity-induced loop currents for cuprate superconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) in cuprate superconductors caused by inhomogeneities from dopants, extending prior work by incorporating local correlations via the unrestricted Gutzwiller approximation and next-nearest neighbor hopping. Correlations suppress loop currents, but the Gutzwiller approach sustains them at higher on-site repulsion compared to Hartree-Fock, enabling estimation of local magnetic moments from impurity-induced currents.
AI.motivation: To understand how local correlations and next-nearest neighbor hopping affect time-reversal symmetry breaking loop currents induced by dopant inhomogeneities in cuprate superconductors, and to extend the TRSB phase toward half-filling.
AI.method: The unrestricted Gutzwiller approximation is used to include local correlations, extending prior Hartree-Fock-based studies. The effects of next-nearest neighbor hopping are also investigated.
AI.result: Correlations generally suppress loop currents, but the Gutzwiller approach sustains such states at larger on-site repulsion than Hartree-Fock. Next-nearest neighbor hopping extends the TRSB phase toward half-filling.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an estimation of local magnetic moments from impurity-induced loop currents in cuprate superconductors, showing that correlations play a key role in the stability of TRSB states.

title: Microwave Studies of Single Crystal TeO2 at Cryogenic Temperatures
summary: We use whispering-gallery-mode analysis to characterise the microwave dielectric properties of single-crystal TeO$_2$ at cryogenic temperatures and compare its loss performance with other low-loss dielectric materials. Finite-element modelling is combined with measurements at room temperature, 4 K, and 20 mK to develop accurate cryogenic simulations and extract the anisotropic dielectric permittivities, giving $\varepsilon_\parallel=25.75\pm0.08$ and $\varepsilon_\perp=20.90\pm0.07$. Loss measurements reveal quality factors as high as $9\times10^6$ and minimum loss tangents approaching $3\times10^{-8}$, placing TeO$_2$ among promising low-loss dielectrics for cryogenic microwave applications. Electron-spin-resonance spectroscopy further indicates a clean spin environment, while identifying distinct spin systems consistent with the known properties of the crystal.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the cryogenic microwave dielectric properties of single-crystal TeO₂ using whispering-gallery-mode analysis, finding high quality factors (up to 9×10⁶) and very low loss tangents (~3×10⁻⁸), with extracted anisotropic permittivities (ε∥=25.75, ε⊥=20.90), positioning TeO₂ as a promising low-loss dielectric for cryogenic microwave applications.
AI.motivation: To characterize the microwave dielectric properties of single-crystal TeO₂ at cryogenic temperatures and evaluate its suitability as a low-loss dielectric material for cryogenic microwave applications, compared to other existing low-loss dielectrics.
AI.method: Whispering-gallery-mode analysis combined with finite-element modeling at room temperature, 4 K, and 20 mK; electron-spin-resonance spectroscopy for spin environment characterization.
AI.result: Extracted anisotropic dielectric permittivities: ε∥=25.75±0.08 and ε⊥=20.90±0.07; quality factors up to 9×10⁶; minimum loss tangents approaching 3×10⁻⁸; clean spin environment with distinct spin systems.
AI.conclusion: TeO₂ is a promising low-loss dielectric for cryogenic microwave applications, with high quality factors and very low loss tangents.

title: Emergent Topology from Nonlocal Electronic Correlations in One Dimension
comment: Main text:7 pages and 3 figures, Supplementary Material: 6 pages and 4 figures
summary: We demonstrate that electronic correlations in low-dimensional systems can induce topological phases starting from a topologically trivial noninteracting band structure. Using an advanced cluster-diagrammatic many-body approach applied to the one-dimensional extended Hubbard model, we show that tuning the nonlocal Coulomb interaction drives the emergence of bond-order-wave (BOW) and charge-density-wave (CDW) phases. Despite being interaction-driven and symmetry-broken, these states admit an effective low-energy single-particle description. In particular, the BOW phase maps onto an effective Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, while the CDW phase, with subleading bond-order correlations, corresponds to a Rice-Mele model. Both phases exhibit a nontrivial topological character, manifested by the presence of localized edge states. Our results establish a mechanism by which nonlocal electronic correlations generate emergent topology in correlated systems.

AI.tldr: Electronic correlations in low-dimensional systems can induce topological phases from trivial band structures. Using a cluster-diagrammatic method on the 1D extended Hubbard model, tuning nonlocal Coulomb interactions drives BOW and CDW phases, which map onto SSH and Rice-Mele models respectively, exhibiting nontrivial topology with localized edge states.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that electronic correlations in low-dimensional systems can generate topological phases even when starting from a topologically trivial noninteracting band structure.
AI.method: Advanced cluster-diagrammatic many-body approach applied to the one-dimensional extended Hubbard model, tuning the nonlocal Coulomb interaction.
AI.result: Tuning nonlocal Coulomb interactions drives emergence of bond-order-wave (BOW) and charge-density-wave (CDW) phases. BOW maps onto an effective SSH model, CDW (with subleading bond-order correlations) maps onto a Rice-Mele model. Both phases show nontrivial topological character with localized edge states.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal electronic correlations provide a mechanism to generate emergent topology in correlated systems, producing topological phases from trivial noninteracting band structures.

title: Perpendicular magnetic anisotropy tuning of macrospin-to-vortex transitions in Co-based artificial spin-vortex ice
summary: We investigate the macrospin-to-vortex (MS-to-V) transition in Co-based artificial spin-vortex ice (ASVI) in the presence of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) by spin-wave spectroscopy. Detailed micromagnetic simulations using mumax3 reveal that the PMA modifies the magnetic energy landscape and facilitates vortex formation, suggesting that PMA can enhance the transition probability. To seek experimental validation of this hypothesis, we prepared Ti (3 nm)/Co (10 nm)/Ti (3 nm)/Pt (2 nm) (TCT) and Ti (3 nm)/Co (10 nm)/Pt (2 nm) (TCP) multilayer stacks. Vibrating sample magnetometry measurements confirm that the TCP film exhibits a larger PMA than the TCT film. Using these stacks, we then investigate the MS-to-V transition probability in ASVIs and found that TCP ASVIs exhibit a higher transition probability than TCT ASVIs, in agreement with the simulation prediction. These findings identify PMA as an effective design parameter for controlling vortex formation in ASVIs and provide a promising route toward task-dependent tuning of fading-memory properties for physical reservoir computing based on artificial spin lattices.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) enhances the macrospin-to-vortex transition in Co-based artificial spin-vortex ice (ASVI), confirmed by both simulations and experiments, demonstrating PMA as a control parameter for vortex formation with implications for physical reservoir computing.
AI.motivation: To understand and control the macrospin-to-vortex transition in artificial spin-vortex ice, and to identify PMA as a design parameter for tuning vortex formation, which is relevant for reservoir computing applications.
AI.method: Micromagnetic simulations (mumax3) to study PMA effects on MS-to-V transition; experimental validation using Ti/Co/Ti/Pt (TCT) and Ti/Co/Pt (TCP) multilayer stacks with VSM measurements to compare PMA and transition probabilities.
AI.result: Simulations show PMA modifies the energy landscape and facilitates vortex formation. TCP films exhibit larger PMA than TCT films, and TCP ASVIs show higher macrospin-to-vortex transition probability, matching simulations.
AI.conclusion: PMA is an effective design parameter for controlling vortex formation in ASVIs, offering a path toward task-dependent tuning of fading-memory properties for physical reservoir computing based on artificial spin lattices.

title: Magnetic control of Goos-Hänchen shifts and group delay time in monolayer WSe$_2$
summary: We study the influence of an external magnetic field on the Goos-Hänchen (GH) shift and the group delay time (GDT) in monolayer WSe$_2$ in the presence of a magnetic barrier. The transport properties of Dirac-like carriers are obtained by solving the effective low-energy Hamiltonian and evaluating the corresponding transmission amplitudes. The GH shift and the GDT are subsequently extracted from the phase of the transmission coefficient. We systematically analyze their dependence on the magnetic field strength, incident energy, angle of incidence, and barrier width, with particular emphasis on the spin and valley degrees of freedom associated with the $K$ and $K'$ valleys. Our results show that the magnetic barrier strongly modulates both the GH shift and the GDT, leading to oscillatory behavior and pronounced spin-valley-dependent transport characteristics. Remarkably, the magnetic field enables selective control of the lateral shift and traversal time of carriers for each spin and valley channel, allowing for tunable spatial and temporal separation of electronic wave packets. This provides a mechanism for manipulating fermionic trajectories after transmission through the barrier in a highly controllable manner. Such tunability opens promising avenues for designing nanoscale devices based on spin and valley filtering, as well as for potential applications in information storage and processing within spintronic and valleytronic platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how an external magnetic field affects the Goos-Hänchen shift and group delay time in monolayer WSe₂ with a magnetic barrier, revealing strong spin-valley-dependent modulation that enables selective control of lateral shifts and traversal times for potential spintronic and valleytronic applications.
AI.motivation: To understand and exploit the influence of a magnetic field on the GH shift and GDT in monolayer WSe₂, aiming to achieve spin and valley control for nanoscale device applications.
AI.method: Solving the effective low-energy Hamiltonian for Dirac-like carriers in monolayer WSe₂ with a magnetic barrier, calculating transmission amplitudes, and extracting GH shift and GDT from the transmission coefficient phase.
AI.result: The magnetic barrier strongly modulates the GH shift and GDT, producing oscillatory behavior and pronounced spin-valley-dependent characteristics, enabling tunable spatial and temporal separation of electronic wave packets.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic field provides controllable spin and valley filtering with tunable lateral shifts and traversal times, offering pathways for spintronic and valleytronic devices in information storage and processing.

title: Bright and Dark Excitons in CrSBr: Local Ligand-Field Character and Band-Coherent Optical Selection Rules
summary: Magnetic van der Waals semiconductors such as CrSBr host an intricate exciton landscape whose physical interpretation has converged only recently. A many-body Feynman diagrammatic approach based on quasiparticle self-consistent GW with electron-hole ladder vertex corrections to the screened Coulomb interaction has established the electronic band gap, excitonic orbital character, real-space extent, binding energies, and bosonic-coupling signatures of the bright XA exciton near 1.34 eV and the higher XB manifold near 1.8 eV. These results agree well with ARPES and magneto-optical experiments and supersede the early Rydberg-like assignment of the excitons. What has remained unresolved is why these intense bright excitons coexist, within a few tens of meV, with companion states that are several orders of magnitude darker despite drawing from essentially the same single-particle transition manifold. Here we show that brightness is a band-coherent property of the excitonic eigenfunctions: bright and dark partners are sublattice-symmetric and sublattice-antisymmetric superpositions of the same ligand-field-like Bloch transitions across the two Cr atoms of the orthorhombic primitive cell. The commonly used Frenkel and Wannier-Mott labels describe what an exciton is made of, but brightness requires a symmetry-adapted interference rule between transition dipoles. Disentangling this bare excitonic structure is a prerequisite for interpreting the optical response of CrSBr once magnon, phonon, and photon couplings are included.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves why bright and dark excitons coexist in CrSBr despite originating from similar single-particle transitions, showing that brightness is a band-coherent property governed by sublattice symmetry: bright excitons are sublattice-symmetric superpositions, dark ones are sublattice-antisymmetric, requiring a symmetry-adapted interference rule beyond Frenkel/Wannier-Mott labels.
AI.motivation: To resolve the unresolved puzzle of why intense bright excitons in CrSBr coexist with companion dark states (orders of magnitude darker) within a few tens of meV, despite drawing from essentially the same single-particle transition manifold.
AI.method: Many-body Feynman diagrammatic approach based on quasiparticle self-consistent GW with electron-hole ladder vertex corrections to the screened Coulomb interaction, combined with symmetry analysis of sublattice-symmetric vs sublattice-antisymmetric superpositions of ligand-field-like Bloch transitions across the two Cr atoms.
AI.result: Brightness is a band-coherent property: bright and dark excitons are respectively sublattice-symmetric and sublattice-antisymmetric superpositions of the same ligand-field-like Bloch transitions. Brightness requires a symmetry-adapted interference rule between transition dipoles, not just Frenkel/Wannier-Mott classification.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling this bare excitonic structure (symmetry-encoded brightness rule) is a prerequisite for interpreting the optical response of CrSBr once magnon, phonon, and photon couplings are included.

title: Layer-resolved Electronic Structure and Correlation of Low-$n$ Square-planar Nickelates: A DFT+DMFT Prediction of Superconducting Candidates
summary: Multi-layer square-planar nickelates provide a rare platform in which the nominal Ni valence, dimensionality, and layer-resolved electronic structure can be tuned within the same structural family. Recent experiments have found superconductivity in $n=4$--8 $R_{n+1}Ni_nO_{2n+2}$ compounds, with the highest $T_c$ near $n=6$, whereas the more heavily hole-doped $n=3$ member remains nonsuperconducting. Here we propose spacer-layer Cl doping as a route to convert low-$n$ nickelates into superconducting candidates. Compared with changing the layer number $n$, Cl substitution on the spacer-layer oxygen sites offers a chemically natural way to continuously tune the Ni valence while leaving the NiO$_2$ planes largely intact; the lower-$n$ compounds may also be more accessible for synthesis. Using density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory, we show that electron-compensated $n=2$ and $n=3$ La-based nickelates, targeted to the nominal Ni valence of superconducting $n=6$, develop Ni-$d$ correlations comparable to those of superconducting higher-$n$ compounds while preserving the characteristic low-energy Ni-$d$ electronic structure. These results suggest spacer-layer Cl doping as a promising strategy for designing low-$n$ square-planar nickelate superconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes spacer-layer Cl doping as a strategy to convert low-n (n=2,3) square-planar nickelates into superconductors, using DFT+DMFT to show that electron-compensated Cl-doped compounds achieve Ni-d correlations and electronic structure comparable to superconducting higher-n members.
AI.motivation: Superconductivity has been observed in n=4-8 R_{n+1}Ni_nO_{2n+2} nickelates with highest Tc near n=6, while the more hole-doped n=3 member remains nonsuperconducting. The authors aim to find a route to induce superconductivity in low-n nickelates.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) is used to study the electronic structure and correlations of Cl-doped n=2 and n=3 La-based nickelates, with the Cl substitution occurring on spacer-layer oxygen sites.
AI.result: Electron-compensated n=2 and n=3 Cl-doped nickelates, tuned to the nominal Ni valence of superconducting n=6, develop Ni-d correlations comparable to higher-n superconducting compounds and preserve the characteristic low-energy Ni-d electronic structure.
AI.conclusion: Spacer-layer Cl doping is a promising strategy for designing low-n square-planar nickelate superconductors, offering a chemically natural way to tune Ni valence continuously while keeping NiO2 planes intact and potentially easier synthesis.

title: The charge density fluctuations and the Shrinking Fermi Liquid scenario for strange metallicity in cuprates
summary: We interpret the strange metal (SM) properties of slightly overdoped cuprates in terms of the recently proposed Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory. This is based on the pervading presence in the cuprate phase diagram of charge density fluctuations (CDF), which have been identified and characterized in RIXS. These fluctuations are abundant and have a low energy due to the proximity of the charge density wave quantum critical point hidden under the superconducting dome of cuprates, but have a short range and non-critical character with a finite energy M/γ~10 meV as measured above Tc. Here M~ ξ^-2 is determined by the short correlation length ξ, while γencodes the Landau damping ruling the lifetime of the charge fluctuations. Besides these low energy CDF, cuprates also display phonons and a broad continuum of particle-hole excitations, mostly due to spin paramagnons arising from their strongly correlated character. With these experimentally characterized ingredients we show that above Tc the SM properties in transport are well described in terms of fermionic Landau quasiparticles scattering with CDF and phonons. The optical properties can instead be interpreted by the combined effect of low energy CDF determining the temperature dependence, and of the paramagnon continuum determining a linear in frequency scattering rate. Remarkably, the combined effect of these simple ingredients also induces ω/T scaling properties for frequencies larger than M/γ. When superconductivity is suppressed by strong magnetic fields the SM properties extend down to a few Kelvin. By assuming that the CDF dissipation parameter γgrows logarithmically by lowering T, we account for all anomalous transport and thermodynamic properties of cuprates (specific heat, Seebeck, heat transport, resistivity, and magnetoresistance) thereby providing a consistent scenario for the SM phase of cuprates.

AI.tldr: This paper explains the strange metal properties of overdoped cuprates using the Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory, where charge density fluctuations (CDF) near a quantum critical point, combined with phonons and paramagnons, account for anomalous transport, optical, and thermodynamic behaviors above Tc and under magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified theoretical explanation for the strange metal phase in slightly overdoped cuprates, which exhibits anomalous transport and thermodynamic properties not captured by standard Fermi liquid theory.
AI.method: The Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory is applied, incorporating experimentally characterized charge density fluctuations (CDF), phonons, and spin paramagnon continua. Scattering rates are computed from these ingredients, and the CDF dissipation parameter γ is assumed to grow logarithmically at low temperatures to extend the theory to high-field regimes.
AI.result: Above Tc, strange metal transport properties are reproduced by Landau quasiparticles scattering with CDF and phonons. Optical properties arise from low-energy CDF (temperature dependence) and paramagnons (linear-in-frequency scattering). ω/T scaling emerges for frequencies above M/γ ≈ 10 meV. Under strong magnetic fields, logarithmic growth of γ explains anomalous specific heat, Seebeck, heat transport, resistivity, and magnetoresistance down to a few Kelvin.
AI.conclusion: The Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory, with CDF, phonons, and paramagnons as key scattering channels, provides a consistent and comprehensive scenario for the strange metal phase of cuprates.

title: Phase stability and ionic transport in post-spinel CaV$_2$O$_4$ cathode
summary: Calcium-ion batteries (CBs) represent an alternative to lithium-ion technology but their advancement is limited by the lack of high-performance intercalation cathodes. Identified via computational screening, post-spinel CaV$_2$O$_4$ has emerged as a promising candidate, though its practical application is hindered by limited electrochemical capacity. Hence, we investigate the thermodynamic and ionic transport characteristics of Ca$_x$V$_2$O$_4$ ($0 \leq x \leq 1$) in this work, by integrating the cluster expansion formalism with Monte Carlo simulations and density functional theory based calculations. We construct the temperature-composition phase diagram of Ca$_x$V$_2$O$_4$ revealing several stable phases ($α$ through $ζ$) that can appear during electrochemical operations at different voltages. Importantly, we observe the formation of the $\varepsilon$ phase at $x \sim 0.83$ across a 370-590~K temperature window via invariant reactions, which agrees with observations in the experimental voltage profiles. Further, migration barrier calculations confirm that Ca mobility is severely impeded within the $α$ ($x \sim 0$) and $γ$ ($x \sim 0.5$) phases. With the strong Ca-vacancy ordering contributing to the high barrier in $γ$ and the persistent two-phase region stretching across the $δ$ ($x \sim 0.67$) and the $γ$ phases, we expect the accessible electrochemical capacity in the CaV$_2$O$_4$ system to be kinetically limited to at most half the theoretical capacity at 298~K, in agreement with experiments. Strategies including cation doping and particle size reduction can be considered to flatten the potential energy landscape of $γ$ and improve Ca mobility. Our computational findings highlight the interplay between stability and transport and provide design strategies that can enable the practical use of CaV$_2$O$_4$ as a CB cathode.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates CaV₂O₄ as a cathode for calcium-ion batteries using computational methods, revealing that Ca mobility is severely limited in certain phases (α and γ) due to strong Ca-vacancy ordering, which restricts practical capacity to at most half the theoretical capacity at 298 K. Strategies like cation doping and particle size reduction are proposed to improve performance.
AI.motivation: Calcium-ion batteries are promising alternatives to lithium-ion technology but are limited by the lack of high-performance intercalation cathodes. Post-spinel CaV₂O₄ was identified as a candidate via computational screening, yet its practical application is hindered by limited electrochemical capacity, motivating the need to understand its thermodynamic and transport properties.
AI.method: The authors integrate cluster expansion formalism with Monte Carlo simulations and density functional theory (DFT) based calculations to study the thermodynamic and ionic transport characteristics of CaₓV₂O₄ (0 ≤ x ≤ 1). They construct temperature-composition phase diagrams and perform migration barrier calculations.
AI.result: The phase diagram reveals several stable phases (α through ζ) during electrochemical operations. The ε phase forms at x ~ 0.83 across 370-590 K, matching experimental voltage profiles. Migration barrier calculations show Ca mobility is severely impeded in α (x ~ 0) and γ (x ~ 0.5) phases. Due to strong Ca-vacancy ordering in γ and a persistent two-phase region spanning δ (x ~ 0.67) and γ phases, the accessible capacity is kinetically limited to at most half the theoretical capacity at 298 K, consistent with experiments.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the interplay between stability and transport in CaV₂O₄, explaining its limited practical capacity. Strategies such as cation doping and particle size reduction are suggested to flatten the potential energy landscape of the γ phase and improve Ca mobility, enabling practical use as a CB cathode.

title: Charge carrier flow through trimmed graphene nanoribbon junctions
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures; supplementary information available as ancillary file (5 additional figures)
summary: As Moore's law approaches its fundamental limits, the development of nanoelectronic devices using low-dimension materials has become a promising avenue for further miniaturization and performance improvements. Among the various novel materials, graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) have emerged as particularly attractive candidates due to their unique electronic properties, opening up a whole new nanoelectronics paradigm consisting of circuits made entirely of graphene. However, due to the technical constraints that naturally arise when working on a two-dimensional plane, the design of efficient nanoelectronic components with a minimal spatial footprint remains a significant challenge. In particular, connecting various components can be a real architectural challenge, comparable to that of the first printed circuit boards. This paper investigates strategies for designing optimal-sized nanoribbon junctions which allow connecting GNRs at an angle, by trimming the junction edge while maintaining favorable electronic properties. Specifically, we show that the probability density current at the tip of junctions is negligible, implying that a selection of atoms can safely be removed without significantly altering the conductance. More generally, we demonstrate that larger trimmings have impacts on the conductance channels, resulting in a conductance that is mainly dictated by the ratio of armchair and zigzag edges. Finally, we propose a simple model relating this ratio to the conductance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates optimal-sized graphene nanoribbon (GNR) junctions for connecting GNRs at an angle, showing that junction tips can be trimmed without significantly affecting conductance, and that conductance is primarily determined by the armchair-to-zigzag edge ratio.
AI.motivation: As Moore's law approaches fundamental limits, there is a need for nanoelectronic devices using low-dimension materials. While graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) are promising for all-graphene circuits, designing efficient nanoelectronic components with minimal spatial footprint is challenging, particularly in connecting components—analogous to early printed circuit board design challenges.
AI.method: The authors investigate design strategies for optimal-sized nanoribbon junctions that connect GNRs at an angle by trimming junction edges. They analyze the probability density current at junction tips and study how trimmings of varying sizes affect conductance channels, developing a model relating the armchair-to-zigzag edge ratio to conductance.
AI.result: The probability density current at junction tips is negligible, allowing safe removal of selected atoms without significantly altering conductance. Larger trimmings impact conductance channels, with conductance mainly dictated by the ratio of armchair and zigzag edges.
AI.conclusion: A simple model relating the armchair-to-zigzag edge ratio to conductance is proposed, enabling optimal-sized GNR junction design for all-graphene nanoelectronic circuits.

title: Heterostructuring as Gateway to Electron Doping of Nickelate Superconductors
comment: The main text spans 6 pages with 4 figures and 1 table, while the Supplemental Material contains 11 pages, 5 figures, and 3 tables. Accepted as an Editors' Suggestions in Physical Review Letters
summary: Despite enormous expenditures in the research field, the electron-doped side of nickelate superconductors remains uncharted territory. Substituting the trivalent rare-earth cations by a tetravalent one hitherto failed. Here, we demonstrate by first-principles calculations a disorder-free route to electron dope Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates. When intercalating wide-band-gap insulating layers such as La$X$O$_3$ ($X$=Al, Ga, Sc) into La$_2$NiO$_4$, the extra (LaO)$^+$ layers act as electron donors, releasing carriers into the Ni-3$d$ orbitals. This electron doping puts La$_2$NiO$_4$:La$_2$AlO$_4$ naturally in the optimal region for $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave superconductivity with T$_c$ exceeding 50 K. The same concept also allows us to electron dope La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, the superconductor in the limelight.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a disorder-free method to electron-dope Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates by intercalating wide-band-gap insulating layers (LaXO₃, X=Al, Ga, Sc), which naturally induces high-Tc superconductivity (exceeding 50 K) in La₂NiO₄ and can also dope La₃Ni₂O₇.
AI.motivation: Electron-doped nickelate superconductors remain unexplored despite significant research investment, as substituting trivalent rare-earth cations with tetravalent ones has failed experimentally.
AI.method: First-principles calculations demonstrate a disorder-free route: intercalating wide-band-gap insulating LaXO₃ (X=Al, Ga, Sc) layers into La₂NiO₄, where extra (LaO)⁺ layers act as electron donors to Ni-3d orbitals.
AI.result: This electron doping places La₂NiO₄:La₂AlO₄ in the optimal region for d_{x²-y²}-wave superconductivity with Tc exceeding 50 K, and the concept extends to electron-doping La₃Ni₂O₇.
AI.conclusion: A viable disorder-free route to achieve electron doping in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates is established, enabling exploration of the electron-doped side of nickelate superconductors.

title: Holographic Theory of Mixed-Dimensional Statistics and Conservation-Encoding Hopping-Operator Algebras
summary:
We develop a general framework for the statistics of mixed-dimensional excitations subject to intertwined conservation laws, extending the familiar Fermi statistics with conserved particle number. We define statistics microscopically through a \emph{hopping-operator algebra}: a local operator subalgebra (LOsA) generated by operators that locally move or deform excitations while preserving the conservation law. Nontrivial statistics arise when this subalgebra is nontrivial.
  We first focus on LOsAs that encode \emph{pointed} conservation laws. These give rise to invertible excitations, whose fusion rules are exactly those of the symmetry defects of a higher group $\cG$. For such $\cG$-conserved excitations in $d$-dimensional space, we show that the corresponding LOsA -- and hence the statistics it defines -- is classified by a cohomology class $[ω] \in H^{d+2}(B\cG;\R/\Z)$, where changing $[ω]$ by a coboundary corresponds merely to a rephasing of the local operators. We further provide a holographic realization: excitations with this prescribed conservation law and statistics live on the boundary of a $\cG$ higher-group gauge theory in $(d+1)$-dimensional space, twisted by $[ω]$.
  More generally, non-pointed conservation laws and the associated statistics of non-invertible excitations are defined by a pair: a LOsA together with its excitation-complex representation. This is equivalent to the pair consisting of a LOsA and its Hilbert-space representation, which is the data defining a generalized symmetry. Consequently, non-pointed conservation laws and their statistics in $d$-dimensional space are classified by fusion $d$-categories, just as generalized symmetries are. The higher-group results above are the fully-pointed special cases of this more general classification.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general framework for statistics of mixed-dimensional excitations under intertwined conservation laws, defining statistics via a hopping-operator algebra (LOsA). Pointed conservation laws yield invertible excitations classified by cohomology $H^{d+2}(B\mathcal{G};\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$, with a holographic realization as boundary excitations of a higher-group gauge theory. More generally, non-pointed conservation laws and non-invertible excitations are classified by fusion $d$-categories, extending the classification of generalized symmetries.
AI.motivation: To extend the familiar Fermi statistics (based on conserved particle number) to a general setting where excitations obey intertwined conservation laws, and to provide a microscopic algebraic framework for defining and classifying the statistics of such mixed-dimensional excitations.
AI.method: Introduces a hopping-operator algebra (local operator subalgebra, LOsA) generated by operators that locally move or deform excitations while preserving conservation laws. Uses cohomological classification for pointed (invertible) cases and fusion $d$-category classification for general (non-invertible) cases. Provides a holographic realization via higher-group gauge theories.
AI.result: Pointed conservation laws with $\mathcal{G}$-conserved excitations in $d$-dimensional space are classified by $[\omega] \in H^{d+2}(B\mathcal{G};\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$, with coboundary changes corresponding to rephasing. Non-pointed cases are classified by fusion $d$-categories, unifying with the classification of generalized symmetries.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies statistics of excitations under intertwined conservation laws, with higher-group results as fully-pointed special cases of a general fusion $d$-category classification, linking directly to generalized symmetries and holographic dualities.

title: Nonlocal Electrostatic Origin of Schottky-Barrier Variability in 2D Contacts
summary: Electrical contacts often limit the performance of atomically thin semiconductor devices. The Schottky barrier height (SBH) is conventionally treated as a local interface property, yet reported values for the same metal/2D-semiconductor contact vary by hundreds of meV. Here we show that, in top contacts, the effective SBH exhibits a pronounced nonlocal electrostatic dependence on defects near the contact edge, beyond the conventional local interface framework. A nonlocal electrostatic model, supported by density-functional-theory-based transport calculations for Ti--MoS$_2$ and Au--MoS$_2$, captures the large, metal-dependent variations in SBH as a function of defect position relative to the contact edge.
