These results provide a unified explanation for the longstanding variability in experimentally extracted SBHs and establish nonlocal electrostatics, mediated by edge-proximal defects, as a key mechanism governing carrier injection in 2D contacts.

AI.tldr: Schottky barrier heights in 2D semiconductor contacts vary widely due to nonlocal electrostatic effects of defects near the contact edge, rather than being a purely local interface property.
AI.motivation: Reported Schottky barrier height (SBH) values for the same metal/2D-semiconductor contact vary by hundreds of meV, lacking a unified explanation within the conventional local interface framework.
AI.method: A nonlocal electrostatic model supported by density-functional-theory-based transport calculations for Ti–MoS₂ and Au–MoS₂ contacts.
AI.result: The effective SBH exhibits a pronounced nonlocal electrostatic dependence on defects near the contact edge, capturing large, metal-dependent variations in SBH as a function of defect position.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal electrostatics mediated by edge-proximal defects is a key mechanism governing carrier injection in 2D contacts, providing a unified explanation for the longstanding variability in experimentally extracted SBHs.

title: The Radial Distribution Functions of Nanofluids: Molecular Dynamics Simulations
summary: Nanofluids, which are composed of insoluble, stable, and well-dispersed solid particles of nanoscale and/or subnanometer sizes suspended in a base liquid, are the next generation of liquids of today. The purpose of this paper is to investigate the one dimensional and three dimensional angle dependent radial distribution functions RDF and ARDF of polymeric nanofluids made up of nonrigid (soft) nanoparticles and a polymer melt (base fluid) using the molecular dynamics simulation approach and to search the shape stabilities by using these results. For this purpose, we use the nanoparticles of three different sizes: 28, 42, and 56 particles. We research them both within the base fluid and without this polymeric medium for instability analysis. We found that the nanoparticles with 28 atoms show the shape instability inside the base fluid when we increase the system temperature from T=1.2 to T=1.8 and hence, the structure of two concentric spherical shell of the nanoparticle breaks down and as a result the empty vacuum between these inner and the outer shells disappears. In contrast to this findings, the nanoparticles with 42 and 56 atoms show the shape stability inside the base fluid by preserving their concentric shell structures when we rise the system temperature and decrease the affinity between the nanoparticles and the base liquid medium.

AI.tldr: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the one-dimensional and three-dimensional angle-dependent radial distribution functions (RDF and ARDF) of polymeric nanofluids composed of nonrigid (soft) nanoparticles in a polymer melt. Nanoparticles of three sizes (28, 42, and 56 atoms) are analyzed for shape stability with and without the polymeric medium. Results show that 28-atom nanoparticles exhibit shape instability at higher temperatures (T=1.2 to T=1.8), with their concentric spherical shell structure collapsing. In contrast, 42- and 56-atom nanoparticles maintain shape stability, preserving their concentric shell structures under increased temperature and reduced nanoparticle-polymer affinity.
AI.motivation: To investigate the shape stability of polymeric nanofluids composed of nonrigid nanoparticles in a polymer melt by analyzing one-dimensional and three-dimensional angle-dependent radial distribution functions (RDF and ARDF) using molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics simulation approach was used to compute one-dimensional and three-dimensional angle-dependent radial distribution functions (RDF and ARDF) for polymeric nanofluids. Nanoparticles of three sizes (28, 42, and 56 atoms) were studied both within the base fluid (polymer melt) and without it for instability analysis.
AI.result: 28-atom nanoparticles show shape instability inside the base fluid when temperature increases from T=1.2 to T=1.8, causing the two concentric spherical shell structure to break down and the vacuum between inner and outer shells to disappear. 42- and 56-atom nanoparticles maintain shape stability, preserving concentric shell structures under increased temperature and decreased nanoparticle-base fluid affinity.
AI.conclusion: Shape stability of polymeric nanofluids depends on nanoparticle size: smaller nanoparticles (28 atoms) are susceptible to shape instability at elevated temperatures, while larger nanoparticles (42 and 56 atoms) exhibit stable concentric shell structures.

title: Vortex Dynamics in Magic-Angle Twisted Graphene
summary: We use a gate-defined Josephson junction (JJ) device made from twisted-layer graphene for studying vortex dynamics in two dimensions. The JJ sensor signals the presence of individual vortices in the superconducting leads nearby the junction through shifts in the Fraunhofer interference pattern of the magnetic-field-dependent critical current $I_c(B)$ across the junction. Rapid vortex fluctuations manifest as telegraph-type noise in time traces of the junction voltage $V(t)$. Measurements of $I_c(B)$ and $V(t)$ are interpreted in terms of multi-vortex processes where fast vortex fluctuations in the leads are modulated by quasi-stationary vortices trapped in the leads. The different timescales associated with these processes allow for their disentangling and quantitative analysis. Tracking the temperature dependence of the vortex-dynamical rates between $T = 7$ mK and $T = 120$ mK, we find that the creep type vortex motion is thermally activated above $T \approx 100$ mK, while the saturation of rates below $T \approx 80$ mK is suggestive of a sharp transition to macroscopic quantum tunneling of vortices.

AI.tldr: Using a twisted-layer graphene Josephson junction device, the paper studies 2D vortex dynamics by detecting individual vortices via Fraunhofer pattern shifts and telegraph noise, revealing thermally activated vortex creep above ~100 mK and evidence of macroscopic quantum tunneling below ~80 mK.
AI.motivation: To investigate vortex dynamics in two dimensions using a novel gate-defined Josephson junction device made from twisted-layer graphene, enabling detection of individual vortices and analysis of their fluctuation mechanisms at millikelvin temperatures.
AI.method: A gate-defined twisted-layer graphene JJ sensor detects individual vortices through shifts in the Fraunhofer interference pattern of I_c(B). Rapid vortex fluctuations are observed as telegraph-type noise in V(t). Multi-vortex processes with distinct timescales are disentangled for quantitative analysis of vortex dynamics.
AI.result: Vortex creep is thermally activated above ~100 mK; below ~80 mK, rate saturation suggests a sharp transition to macroscopic quantum tunneling of vortices.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a crossover from thermally activated vortex creep to macroscopic quantum tunneling at low temperatures, enabled by the graphene JJ sensor's ability to resolve individual vortex dynamics across timescales.

title: Accurate Self-Attention Wavefunctions at Large Scale
summary: Self-attention neural networks provide powerful variational wavefunctions that surpass the expressivity of traditional variational ansatze. This expressivity, however, comes with increased computational complexity, raising a pressing question about scalability -- can such wavefunctions retain their accuracy at large system sizes? We apply self-attention wavefunctions to the two-dimensional homogeneous electron gas for up to N=169 particles, obtaining energies systematically lower than state-of-the-art DMC. Direct access to the ground state wavefunction further lets us recover the full collective-mode dispersion of the liquid phase, from the small-q plasmon branch to a roton-like minimum near q=2k_F. Observables at N=91 and N=169 are in near-perfect agreement, indicating convergence to the thermodynamic limit.

AI.tldr: Self-attention neural network wavefunctions are applied to the 2D homogeneous electron gas for up to N=169 particles, achieving lower energies than state-of-the-art DMC, recovering the full collective-mode dispersion, and demonstrating convergence to the thermodynamic limit.
AI.motivation: To address whether self-attention wavefunctions retain their accuracy at large system sizes despite their increased computational complexity, and to test scalability in the 2D homogeneous electron gas.
AI.method: Self-attention neural network variational wavefunctions applied to the two-dimensional homogeneous electron gas for system sizes up to N=169 particles.
AI.result: Energies systematically lower than state-of-the-art DMC; full collective-mode dispersion recovered (from small-q plasmon branch to roton-like minimum near q=2k_F); near-perfect agreement between observables at N=91 and N=169.
AI.conclusion: Self-attention wavefunctions scale effectively to large system sizes and converge to the thermodynamic limit, demonstrating strong potential for scalable neural-network-based variational quantum Monte Carlo.

title: Interplay between Electronic Structure, Chemical Bonding, and Lattice Symmetry in Bismuth Vanadate
summary: Bismuth vanadate (BiVO$_4$) is a prototypical oxide photocatalyst that occurs in both tetragonal and monoclinic scheelite phases with markedly different photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical activities. Accurately identifying the monoclinic phase as the ground state and explaining the origin of its symmetry-breaking distortion are unusually challenging from a theoretical perspective, with various levels of theory and associated physical interpretations for this behaviour reported in the literature. Here, we resolve these discrepancies by systematically assessing the role of exact exchange with and without spin-orbit coupling, demonstrating that an accurate treatment of electronic localization is essential to stabilize the monoclinic scheelite structure. Using this framework, we compute the electronic band structure through dense sampling of the Brillouin zone and show that the band edges in monoclinic and tetragonal BiVO$_4$ lie far from conventional high-symmetry paths, leading to substantial differences in band gaps and carrier effective masses. Choosing the exchange-correlation functional that best reproduces the crystal structure leads to excellent predictions of the band gap once excitonic and thermal effects are taken into account. In addition, we show that the monoclinic distortion is driven by charge transfer between non-equivalent oxygen sites, which breaks the lattice symmetry and is suppressed by self-interaction errors when using semi-local DFT. These results establish a direct connection between the exchange-correlation functional, electronic localization, chemical bonding, and structural stability in BiVO$_4$, providing a foundation for robust ab initio descriptions of phase stability and optoelectronic properties in such complex oxides.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves long-standing theoretical discrepancies in identifying the monoclinic phase of BiVO₄ as the ground state, showing that accurate treatment of electronic localization via exact exchange with spin-orbit coupling is essential, and that the monoclinic distortion arises from charge transfer between inequivalent oxygen sites, which is suppressed by self-interaction errors in semi-local DFT.
AI.motivation: To resolve the theoretical discrepancies in accurately identifying the monoclinic scheelite phase of BiVO₄ as the ground state and explaining the origin of its symmetry-breaking distortion, which have proven challenging across different levels of theory.
AI.method: Systematic assessment of exact exchange with and without spin-orbit coupling, dense Brillouin zone sampling for band structure computation, and evaluation of exchange-correlation functionals to connect electronic localization, structural stability, and optoelectronic properties.
AI.result: An accurate treatment of electronic localization is essential to stabilize the monoclinic scheelite structure; band edges lie far from conventional high-symmetry paths causing substantial differences in band gaps and carrier effective masses; monoclinic distortion is driven by charge transfer between non-equivalent oxygen sites and is suppressed by self-interaction errors in semi-local DFT.
AI.conclusion: There is a direct connection between the exchange-correlation functional, electronic localization, chemical bonding, and structural stability in BiVO₄, providing a foundation for robust ab initio descriptions of phase stability and optoelectronic properties in complex oxides.

title: Curvature-Controlled Topological Magnon Phases in a Folded Kagome Lattice
summary: We show that geometric curvature, encoded in the folding angle between two corner-sharing triangles on a kagome lattice, provides a continuous tuning knob for topological magnon phase. Starting from an extended spin Hamiltonian with exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction, and a higher-order bow-tie coupling of scalar chiralities, we derive the chirality-mediated hopping amplitude, which depends on the folding and spin canting of the bow-tie triangles. At small folding and canting angles, the bow-tie coupling surpasses DM, establishing a curvature-dominated regime. These results establish curvature as an intrinsic geometric control parameter for topological magnonics and reveal a direct analogy with chirality-induced spin selectivity in molecular systems, pointing to a unified mechanism for chirality driven transport across scales. The mechanism is particularly relevant for chiral crystals where the DM interaction is weak or forbidden by symmetry, as in systems with a six-fold screw axis.

AI.tldr: Geometric curvature (folding angle on kagome lattice) serves as a continuous tuning knob for topological magnon phases. A chirality-mediated hopping amplitude, derived from extended spin Hamiltonians, dominates over Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction at small angles, establishing a curvature-driven regime analogous to chirality-induced spin selectivity.
AI.motivation: To establish geometric curvature as an intrinsic control parameter for topological magnonics, especially relevant for chiral crystals where DM interaction is weak or symmetry-forbidden.
AI.method: Derivation of chirality-mediated hopping amplitude from an extended spin Hamiltonian (exchange, DM, bow-tie coupling) on a kagome lattice, analyzing the dependence on folding and spin canting angles.
AI.result: At small folding and canting angles, bow-tie coupling surpasses DM interaction, creating a curvature-dominated regime where geometric curvature tunes topological magnon phases continuously.
AI.conclusion: Curvature is an intrinsic geometric control parameter for topological magnonics, with a direct analogy to chirality-induced spin selectivity in molecular systems, suggesting a unified chirality-driven transport mechanism across scales.

title: Valley Hall viscosity in the integer quantum Hall phases of (2+1)D Dirac materials
summary: We calculate the valley-resolved Hall viscosity for Lorentz-invariant integer quantum Hall phases in Semenoff-semiconducting graphene-like systems at zero temperature. The Kubo formalism based discussion reported in Phys. Rev. B 100, 115421 (2019) revealed the divergence of single valley viscous Hall contributions for this case with only a valley-summed Hall viscosity being finite and therefore well-defined. Our approach to the Hall viscosity calculation is based on an equivalent Green function formulation within Wigner-Weyl calculus. We find that the previously identified divergence seems to be regularized to a finite value in a proper representation of the valley-resolved Hall viscosity in terms of energy eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. Together with the local Hall conductivity and its first nonlocal correction, reported as well in Phys. Rev. B 100, 115421 (2019), we extend the empirical relativistic Hoyos-Son formula to individual valleys. Both the original Hoyos-Son formula for Galilean invariant fluids and its relativistic extension to Dirac materials are found to be structurally identical for integer quantum Hall phases and expressible in terms of local electric and viscous Hall responses. In addition we evaluate the valley(-difference) Hall viscosity for biased Bernal bilayer graphene in the chiral fermion low energy approximation. Prospects of measuring valley Hall viscosity in nonlocal transport for mono- and bilayer graphene- and group-VI TMD-based devices are discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper calculates valley-resolved Hall viscosity in graphene-like systems, shows that previously reported divergences are regularized when using proper eigenfunction representations, extends the relativistic Hoyos-Son formula to individual valleys, evaluates valley Hall viscosity in biased Bernal bilayer graphene, and discusses experimental prospects for measuring valley Hall viscosity in nonlocal transport.
AI.motivation: To resolve the divergence issue in single-valley Hall viscosity reported in prior work (Phys. Rev. B 100, 115421) and to extend the Hoyos-Son formula to individual valleys in relativistic Dirac systems.
AI.method: Green function formulation within Wigner-Weyl calculus; representation of Hall viscosity in terms of energy eigenfunctions and eigenvalues.
AI.result: The previously identified divergence in single-valley Hall viscosity is regularized to a finite value. The relativistic Hoyos-Son formula is structurally identical for integer quantum Hall phases in both Galilean and Dirac systems. Valley Hall viscosity is evaluated for biased Bernal bilayer graphene.
AI.conclusion: Valley Hall viscosity can be measured in nonlocal transport in mono- and bilayer graphene and group-VI TMD-based devices.

title: Magnetophonon Resistance Oscillations in Structures with a GaAs Quantum Well and Barriers of AlAs/GaAs$\langleδ$-Si$\rangle$ Superlattices
summary: Magnetophonon resistance oscillations (MPR) associated with the resonant scattering of electrons by optical phonons at temperatures of 77-240 K, as well as resonant scattering of electrons by acoustic phonons (PIRO) at temperatures of 10-25 K, were investigated in the same samples featuring a GaAs quantum well and AlAs/GaAs superlattice barriers doped with Si. The study of MPR demonstrated that resonant electron scattering occurs on bulk longitudinal optical phonons and does not depend on the dimensionality of the system or inter-subband transitions in systems with two subbands of size quantization. However, the amplitude of the oscillation with number $N=1$ in two-dimensional structures depends on the interplay of scattering mechanisms, which, in turn, is influenced by the structure of the system. As for PIRO, in samples with two size quantization subbands, resonant electron scattering by longitudinal acoustic phonons is observed against the background of inter-subband transitions (MISO), leading to their interference.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates magnetophonon resonance (MPR) oscillations (77-240 K) and phonon-induced resistance oscillations (PIRO, 10-25 K) in GaAs quantum wells with AlAs/GaAs superlattice barriers doped with Si. MPR arises from resonant scattering by bulk longitudinal optical phonons, independent of dimensionality or inter-subband transitions, though the N=1 oscillation amplitude depends on scattering mechanisms tied to system structure. PIRO shows resonant scattering by longitudinal acoustic phonons in samples with two subbands, interfering with magneto-intersubband oscillations (MISO).
AI.motivation: To study electron-phonon resonant scattering mechanisms (optical and acoustic) in the same GaAs quantum well samples with two size quantization subbands, clarifying the role of dimensionality, subband structure, and interference effects.
AI.method: Magnetotransport measurements of MPR (77-240 K) and PIRO (10-25 K) in GaAs quantum wells with AlAs/GaAs superlattice barriers doped with Si, analyzing oscillation amplitudes and interference patterns.
AI.result: MPR is mediated by bulk LO phonons, independent of system dimensionality and inter-subband transitions; N=1 amplitude depends on scattering mechanisms and system structure. PIRO involves resonant scattering by LA phonons in two-subband samples, interfering with MISO.
AI.conclusion: Resonant electron scattering by longitudinal optical phonons is bulk-like and dimension-independent, while acoustic phonon scattering in two-subband systems leads to observable interference with inter-subband transitions.

title: Quantum-Geometric Design of Lattice Generalized Landau Levels
summary: We design lattice models with tailored quantum geometry, including generalized Landau levels (LLs) satisfying the integrated trace condition and higher-Chern bands with ideal quantum geometry. Our models with $N=2$, $3$, and $4$ sublattices include a generalized Haldane model ($N=2$ honeycomb lattice model) with Gaussian-decaying hoppings realizable in twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$, and $N \geq 3$ models with exponentially decaying hoppings. Exact diagonalization reveals fractional Chern insulators in the generalized zeroth LL bands of all three models, a Moore-Read state in the generalized first LL band of the $N=4$ model, and various interaction-driven topological phases$\unicode{x2013}$including integer and fractional anomalous Hall crystals and a multicomponent Halperin state$\unicode{x2013}$in the ideal higher-Chern band of the $N=3$ model. Informed by quantum geometry, our work provides a pathway for lattice realizations of Landau-level and beyond-Landau-level physics.

AI.tldr: The paper designs lattice models with tailored quantum geometry to realize Landau-level and beyond-Landau-level physics, demonstrating fractional Chern insulators, Moore-Read states, and various topological phases through exact diagonalization.
AI.motivation: To create lattice models that can realize the quantum geometry of Landau levels and beyond, enabling fractional Chern insulators and other topological phases that are typically challenging to achieve in lattice systems.
AI.method: Design of lattice models (N=2,3,4 sublattices) with tailored quantum geometry including generalized Landau levels satisfying integrated trace condition and higher-Chern bands with ideal quantum geometry, using Gaussian-decaying (twisted bilayer MoTe₂ motivated) and exponentially decaying hoppings, analyzed via exact diagonalization.
AI.result: Fractional Chern insulators in generalized zeroth LL bands (all models); Moore-Read state in generalized first LL band (N=4 model); integer and fractional anomalous Hall crystals and multicomponent Halperin state in ideal higher-Chern band (N=3 model).
AI.conclusion: Quantum geometry-informed lattice models provide a systematic pathway for realizing Landau-level physics and exotic topological phases beyond conventional Landau levels in lattice systems.

title: Quantum weight and low-loss EELS signatures of Wannier quantum geometry in black phosphorus
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures from results of codes used , 3 figures schematic from tikz code
summary: Quantum geometry is now experimentally accessible in crystalline solids, with black phosphorus providing a key platform through polarization-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. We develop a first-principles framework that connects the momentum-resolved quantum metric of black phosphorus to a complementary bulk observable: the direction-resolved quantum weight measurable through low-loss electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS). A 32-band DFT--Wannier Hamiltonian is used to compute both single-band and occupied-manifold geometric quantities from analytic momentum derivatives. We show that the raw single-band quantum metric of the top valence band is not globally meaningful in the conventional cell because folding degeneracies and intra-valence near degeneracies produce true isolated-band singularities; masked maps and occupied-manifold projectors are therefore essential. Because semilocal PBE produces near-gap semimetallic pockets and spurious subgap interpolation features, we introduce an experimentally motivated restricted quantum weight $K_{ii}(ω_c)$, which obeys the corresponding restricted Souza--Wilkens--Martin sum rule and is the appropriate quantity for low-loss EELS once the zero-loss region is excluded. The restricted in-plane quantum weight is nearly isotropic, $K_{zz}/K_{xx}=0.972\pm0.005$ (armchair/zigzag), despite the strong band-mass anisotropy and armchair-only absorption onset of black phosphorus. Orbital-resolved Hubbard--Hartree corrections leave the absolute quantum weights rigid at the sub-percent level while producing a small but resolved armchair-directed drift of $K_{zz}/K_{xx}$, approximately $+0.46\%$ per eV of $U$. These results identify low-loss EELS spectral moments as a practical probe of integrated quantum geometry in an anisotropic layered material.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a first-principles framework linking the momentum-resolved quantum metric of black phosphorus to a direction-resolved quantum weight measurable via low-loss EELS, finding nearly isotropic in-plane quantum weight despite strong electronic anisotropy, with Hubbard corrections introducing small directional drift.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between momentum-resolved quantum geometry (accessible via ARPES) and bulk-integrated observables (accessible via EELS), and to demonstrate how low-loss EELS spectral moments can serve as a practical probe of integrated quantum geometry in anisotropic layered materials.
AI.method: A 32-band DFT-Wannier Hamiltonian is constructed for black phosphorus. Single-band and occupied-manifold quantum geometric quantities are computed using analytic momentum derivatives. A restricted quantum weight K_ii(ω_c) is introduced with a corresponding Souza-Wilkens-Martin sum rule, designed for low-loss EELS excluding the zero-loss region. Orbital-resolved Hubbard-Hartree corrections are applied to assess many-body effects.
AI.result: The restricted in-plane quantum weight is nearly isotropic (K_zz/K_xx = 0.972±0.005), despite strong band-mass anisotropy and armchair-only absorption onset. Hubbard corrections leave absolute quantum weights rigid at sub-percent level but produce a small armchair-directed drift of ~+0.46% per eV of U.
AI.conclusion: Low-loss EELS spectral moments can probe integrated quantum geometry in anisotropic layered materials, and the restricted quantum weight formalism is appropriate when the zero-loss region is excluded.

title: Competing Chern states revealed by quasiparticle charging in moiré rhombohedral graphene
summary: Moiré materials realize a versatile platform for exploring the physics of fractional Chern insulators (FCIs). The recently observed evolution from FCIs to an extended quantum anomalous Hall background upon lowering the electronic temperature in moiré rhombohedral graphene (mRG)8 raises a fundamental question: Is it caused by a failure to equilibrate the edge states of an FCI or by a genuine phase transition in the bulk from an FCI to a generalized anomalous Hall crystal? Here we address this question by probing quasiparticle charging in a mesoscopic mRG antidot device and by bulk resistance measurements, both of which are bulk-sensitive and free from complications from edge states. Tunneling to the mRG antidot reveals quasiparticles carrying one electron charge for both Chern states at filling factors ν=1 and 2/3 at low temperatures. Temperature dependence measurements of the bulk resistance near ν=2/3 further suggest a thermodynamic phase transition from an FCI to a generalized anomalous Hall crystal at temperatures below about 150mK. The results clearly exclude the edge state equilibration scenario and favor the phase transition scenario. Our work establishes mesoscopic probes as a powerful approach to uncover competing ground states in moiré materials and provides a basis for probing fractionalized excitations in FCIs.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a mesoscopic mRG antidot device and bulk resistance measurements to show that the evolution from FCIs to an anomalous Hall background in moiré rhombohedral graphene at low temperatures is due to a thermodynamic phase transition (from FCI to generalized anomalous Hall crystal) rather than edge state equilibration failure.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the observed evolution from FCIs to a quantum anomalous Hall background at lower temperatures in moiré rhombohedral graphene is caused by edge state equilibration failure or a genuine bulk phase transition.
AI.method: Probing quasiparticle charging in a mesoscopic mRG antidot device (tunneling measurements) combined with bulk resistance measurements, both bulk-sensitive and edge-state-free.
AI.result: Quasiparticles carrying one electron charge for both Chern states at ν=1 and 2/3; temperature-dependent bulk resistance near ν=2/3 suggests a thermodynamic phase transition from FCI to generalized anomalous Hall crystal below ~150 mK.
AI.conclusion: The results exclude the edge state equilibration scenario and support the phase transition scenario, establishing mesoscopic probes as a powerful method for studying competing ground states and fractionalized excitations in moiré materials.

title: Exciton valley depolarization in monolayer MoS2: non-Markovian quantum dynamics, intervalley scattering, and the breakdown of the Dyakonov-Perel mechanism
summary: In monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, exciton valley relaxation is typically attributed to the Dyakonov-Perel (DP) mechanism, where frequent intravalley scattering with phonons or defects suppresses the intervalley exchange-induced precession and the role of intervalley scattering is considered secondary. Employing a first-principles nonequilibrium exciton Green's function (NEGF) approach with the generalized Kadanoff-Baym ansatz (GKBA), which treats exchange-driven precession and exciton-phonon scattering on an equal footing across the full Brillouin zone, we demonstrate that even in the small momentum regime most favorable to DP physics, realistic exciton-phonon scattering is too weak to induce the motional narrowing that defines the DP regime. Upon accounting for excitons across the entire Brillouin zone, large momentum intervalley scattering becomes the dominant pathway for valley relaxation, shortening the depolarization by a factor of 3-4 relative to intravalley-only models. We find that valley depolarization and decoherence time are approximately 50 fs at 300 K and lengthen to 130 fs at 10 K. By comparing our results with a Lindblad-type collision framework, we explicitly demonstrate the role of non-Markovian effects and reveal that the Markovian Lindblad framework is highly basis dependent. In the valley-pseudospin basis underlying prior analyses, the Lindblad approach artificially amplifies scattering-induced equilibration, biasing the dynamics toward a DP interpretation. Our study provides a comprehensive picture of valley relaxation, and establishes the exciton density matrix approach derived from NEGF+GKBA as a powerful tool for investigating ultrafast exciton dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using a first-principles NEGF+GKBA approach, the paper shows that exciton valley relaxation in monolayer TMDs is not governed by the Dyakonov-Perel mechanism as previously thought; instead, large-momentum intervalley scattering is the dominant relaxation pathway, with depolarization times of ~50 fs at 300 K and ~130 fs at 10 K. The study also reveals that Markovian Lindblad frameworks are basis-dependent and can artificially bias results toward a DP interpretation.
AI.motivation: To resolve whether the Dyakonov-Perel mechanism (intravalley scattering suppressing exchange-driven precession) or intervalley scattering dominates exciton valley relaxation in monolayer TMDs, and to assess the validity of prior Markovian Lindblad-based analyses.
AI.method: First-principles nonequilibrium exciton Green's function (NEGF) approach with the generalized Kadanoff-Baym ansatz (GKBA), treating exchange-driven precession and exciton-phonon scattering on equal footing across the full Brillouin zone; comparison with a Lindblad-type collision framework to examine non-Markovian and basis-dependent effects.
AI.result: Exciton-phonon scattering is too weak to induce motional narrowing even in the small-momentum regime; large-momentum intervalley scattering dominates valley relaxation, shortening depolarization by a factor of 3-4 vs. intravalley-only models. Valley depolarization/decoherence time is ~50 fs at 300 K and ~130 fs at 10 K. The Lindblad approach is highly basis-dependent and artificially biases toward DP interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Intervalley scattering, not the DP mechanism, is the dominant pathway for exciton valley relaxation in monolayer TMDs. The NEGF+GKBA exciton density matrix approach is established as a powerful tool for studying ultrafast exciton dynamics, and careful treatment of non-Markovian effects and basis choices is essential.

title: PhononScore: a phonon-aware scoring function for dynamical stability
summary: In recent years, crystal generation models have enabled the design of massive numbers of candidate materials. However, the lack of dynamical stability among generated structures has become a major bottleneck preventing their translation into practical materials discovery. To address this challenge, we propose PhononScore, a phonon-aware scoring function for crystal generation. Unlike computationally expensive explicit phonon calculations, PhononScore predicts a unified stability score from crystal structures, enabling ranking of candidate materials dynamical stability with second-level computational cost. We construct a multi-fidelity phonon dataset containing 157,463 crystal structures. On the PhononBench benchmark, PhononScore improves the average dynamical stability rate of candidate pools generated by nine crystal generation models from 30.7% to 83.7%, achieving a 2.72-fold enrichment of stable structures, while the average stability rate of the Top-10 candidates reaches 97.5%. On a high-fidelity DFT-PBE phonon benchmark, the DFT-finetuned PhononScore-DFT increases the Top-100 stability rate to 93.0% and achieves 5-6-fold enrichment of dynamically stable structures under an extremely imbalanced hard-screening scenario. As a materials-screening tool analogous to scoring functions in drug discovery, PhononScore can serve directly as a dynamical-stability feedback signal for crystal generation, active learning, and reinforcement learning, enabling second-level stability-aware reranking without explicit phonon calculations and providing a unified and efficient dynamical stability evaluator for high-throughput materials discovery, active learning, reinforcement learning, and closed-loop inverse design. The online PhononScore platform is available at: http://phononbench.cn/phononscore/

AI.tldr: PhononScore is a phonon-aware scoring function that predicts dynamical stability of crystal structures from structure alone in seconds, improving the stability rate of candidate materials from 30.7% to 83.7% and enabling efficient high-throughput screening.
AI.motivation: Crystal generation models produce massive candidate materials, but lack of dynamical stability assessment is a major bottleneck. Explicit phonon calculations are computationally expensive, hindering practical materials discovery.
AI.method: Constructed a multi-fidelity phonon dataset of 157,463 crystal structures. Developed PhononScore to predict a unified stability score directly from crystal structures, enabling second-level computational cost assessment. Includes a DFT-finetuned version (PhononScore-DFT) for high-fidelity screening.
AI.result: On PhononBench, improves average dynamical stability rate from 30.7% to 83.7% (2.72-fold enrichment); Top-10 candidates reach 97.5% stability rate. PhononScore-DFT achieves 93.0% Top-100 stability rate and 5-6-fold enrichment under hard-screening scenarios.
AI.conclusion: PhononScore serves as a fast, unified dynamical stability evaluator analogous to scoring functions in drug discovery, applicable to crystal generation, active learning, reinforcement learning, and closed-loop inverse design without explicit phonon calculations.

title: A crystal-field route to THz-driven magnetization
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures, 10 supplementary figures, and 2 supplementary tables
summary: Light carries angular momentum, but the microscopic pathways that transform it into magnetization remain elusive. Here we establish that crystal-field excitations, historically viewed primarily as equilibrium spectroscopic fingerprints of localized 4$f$ electrons, constitute an active microscopic route through which circularly-polarized terahertz (THz) light creates magnetic polarization. Using wavelength-selective ultrafast Faraday spectroscopy on the paramagnetic insulator CeF$_3$, we show that resonant excitation of localized 4$f$ crystal-field transitions generates a helicity-dependent magnetization that survives for up to about 100 ps. Most strikingly, while the optical helicity is held fixed, the THz-driven response reverses sign as the excitation wavelength is tuned across the crystal-field resonance. The resulting dispersive spectral response follows the crystal-field excitation spectrum rather than that of optical phonons, and is captured by resonant electronic theory of the inverse Faraday effect. Our results identify crystal-field excitations as a previously unrecognized dynamical reservoir for optical angular momentum and broaden the microscopic pathways through which THz light can create and manipulate magnetic states.

AI.tldr: Crystal-field excitations in CeF₃ serve as an active microscopic pathway for converting circularly-polarized THz light into magnetization via the inverse Faraday effect, with helicity-dependent magnetization lasting ~100 ps and a dispersive spectral response that reverses sign across the crystal-field resonance.
AI.motivation: To identify the microscopic pathways through which light carrying angular momentum transforms into magnetization, specifically investigating whether crystal-field excitations in 4f electron systems can serve as an active route for this conversion.
AI.method: Wavelength-selective ultrafast Faraday spectroscopy on the paramagnetic insulator CeF₃, using circularly-polarized terahertz light to resonantly excite localized 4f crystal-field transitions and measuring helicity-dependent magnetization dynamics.
AI.result: Resonant excitation of crystal-field transitions generates helicity-dependent magnetization lasting ~100 ps; the THz-driven response reverses sign as excitation wavelength is tuned across the crystal-field resonance, producing a dispersive spectral response that follows the crystal-field excitation spectrum rather than optical phonons.
AI.conclusion: Crystal-field excitations represent a previously unrecognized dynamical reservoir for optical angular momentum, broadening the microscopic pathways for THz light to create and manipulate magnetic states in 4f electron systems.

title: Barnett effect generated by a rotating electric field in a ferromagnetic film
summary: We investigate the space-time evolution of the magnetization induced in a 2D ferromagnetic island by a short pulse of a rotating electric field. The field generates elastic twists that act on the magnetization via the Barnett effect: magnetization by rotation. Analytical studies are conducted within classical electrodynamics of continuous media and continuous elastic theory, while numerical studies are performed using discretized Landau-Lifshitz spin dynamics on the atomic lattice. The effect is studied for typical parameters of magnetic oxides at various field frequencies and amplitudes, and for various strengths of magnetic anisotropy, exchange, and damping. The possibility of reversing the island magnetization with an electric-field pulse is demonstrated.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how a short pulse of a rotating electric field can induce and reverse magnetization in a 2D ferromagnetic island via the Barnett effect (magnetization by rotation), using both analytical continuum theories and numerical spin dynamics simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand the space-time evolution of magnetization induced by electric-field pulses in ferromagnetic islands, and to explore the potential for magnetization reversal using electric fields rather than magnetic fields.
AI.method: Analytical methods based on classical electrodynamics of continuous media and continuous elastic theory, combined with numerical simulations using discretized Landau-Lifshitz spin dynamics on an atomic lattice.
AI.result: The effect is characterized across various field frequencies, amplitudes, magnetic anisotropy strengths, exchange couplings, and damping parameters for typical magnetic oxides. Magnetization reversal via an electric-field pulse is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Rotating electric fields can effectively induce and reverse magnetization in ferromagnetic islands through the Barnett effect, offering a potential pathway for electric-field-controlled spintronic devices.

title: An Efficient Method for Gibbs Free Energy Evaluation under Volume Compression
summary: Accurate evaluation of Gibbs free energies is essential for constructing pressure-temperature phase diagrams. Conventional methods based on the quasi-harmonic approximation (QHA) require phonon spectra at many volume points and are therefore expensive in general. Here we develop an efficient method based on the interpolation of a few ab initio data points for Gibbs free energy evaluation under volume compression. Phonon spectra are calculated only at selected volumes. An effective Gruneisen parameter derived from the zero-point energy (ZPE) reconstructs the static-ZPE branch, while piecewise mode-resolved Gruneisen slopes reconstruct the finite-temperature vibrational branches on the target volume grids. The method is validated against QHA benchmarks for diamond (C), Al, Si, Ge, rutile TiO2, beta-PtO2, and Ta2O5 polymorphs. For simple benchmark systems (C, Al, Si, Ge, rutile TiO2, and beta-PtO2), the Gibbs free energy mean absolute errors (MAEs) relative to the QHA benchmarks remain below 0.53 meV/atom, with a six-system average of 0.148 meV/atom, while the number of explicit phonon volume points is reduced from about 20-21 to 3 in the lowest-cost implementation. For the more complex Ta2O5 polymorphs, the reconstructed free energies reproduce the main phase-stability topology despite larger phase-dependent errors. With reference to the QHA workflows, the interpolation method in this work achieves speedups of 5.911-9.023 times and remains reliable for moderate compression ranges where phonon frequencies vary smoothly with volume.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an efficient interpolation method for Gibbs free energy evaluation under volume compression, using phonon spectra at only selected volumes and Gruneisen parameter-based reconstruction, achieving speedups of ~6-9× over QHA with minimal accuracy loss (average MAE 0.148 meV/atom) for simple systems, validated on diamond, Al, Si, Ge, TiO2, PtO2, and Ta2O5.
AI.motivation: Accurate evaluation of Gibbs free energies is essential for pressure-temperature phase diagrams, but conventional QHA methods require phonon spectra at many volume points and are computationally expensive.
AI.method: Phonon spectra are calculated only at selected volumes. An effective Gruneisen parameter from zero-point energy reconstructs the static-ZPE branch, while piecewise mode-resolved Gruneisen slopes reconstruct finite-temperature vibrational branches on target volume grids.
AI.result: For simple systems (C, Al, Si, Ge, rutile TiO2, beta-PtO2), Gibbs free energy MAEs remain below 0.53 meV/atom (six-system average 0.148 meV/atom), reducing explicit phonon volume points from ~20-21 to 3. Speedups of 5.911-9.023× over QHA. For complex Ta2O5 polymorphs, main phase-stability topology is reproduced despite larger errors.
AI.conclusion: The interpolation method achieves significant speedups over QHA while remaining reliable for moderate compression ranges where phonon frequencies vary smoothly with volume.

title: Complex polar superstructure controlled thermal conductivity in ferroelectric PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 11 pages of supporting informatiton
summary: Integrating epitaxial thin films of ferroelectric PbTiO3 and paraelectric SrTiO3 into artificially layered periodic superlattices provides a unique platform for tuning strain, depolarization, and interfacial/surface energies, thereby accessing a rich phase diagram of topological polar structures (skyrmions, vortices, merons, or sinusoidal waves) and superstructures (polar supercrystals). Here we show that the 3D arrangement of polar vortices in a supercrystal suppresses thermal conductivity (k) of PTO/STO superlattices (SLs). The temperature dependence of k reflects the evolution of the polar superstructure, as determined by X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. The comparison with other SLs suggests that the 3D arrangement is crucial for controlling thermal conductivity beyond the usual interfacial scattering. Moreover, we observed an unexpected reduction in thermal conductivity with increasing superlattice thickness, a phenomenon reminiscent of phonon-wave Anderson localization. Our results show that complex polar superstructures can be useful active elements for modulating heat transport in technologies where control over heat dissipation is critical.

AI.tldr: PTO/STO superlattices with 3D polar vortex supercrystal arrangements suppress thermal conductivity via mechanisms beyond interfacial scattering, including thickness-dependent reduction reminiscent of phonon Anderson localization.
AI.motivation: To investigate how complex 3D topological polar structures (vortex supercrystals) in ferroelectric/paraelectric superlattices modulate thermal transport, exploiting the rich phase diagram of polar textures for heat dissipation control.
AI.method: Epitaxial thin films of PbTiO3 and SrTiO3 were grown as artificially layered periodic superlattices; thermal conductivity was measured as a function of temperature and superlattice thickness, correlated with structural characterization via X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
AI.result: The 3D polar vortex supercrystal arrangement suppresses thermal conductivity beyond conventional interfacial scattering. Thermal conductivity decreases with increasing superlattice thickness, an anomalous trend attributed to phonon-wave Anderson localization.
AI.conclusion: Complex polar superstructures serve as active elements for modulating heat transport, offering new strategies for thermal management in technologies requiring controlled heat dissipation.

title: Harnessing orbital Hall effect for energy-efficient magnetization switching in room-temperature van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
summary: 2D van der Waals (vdW) magnets provide new opportunities for spin-orbit torque magnetoresistive random-access memory (SOT-MRAM) due to their unique properties. Electrically manipulating the magnetization of vdW magnets is key to realizing 2D SOT-MRAM, whereas conventional spin Hall materials such as heavy metals and topological insulators suffer from limitations in torque efficiency and energy consumption. Although recent studies show that the orbital Hall conductivity in light metals greatly exceeds the spin Hall conductivity, direct experimental demonstrations that the orbital Hall effect (OHE) can induce more energy-efficient SOT switching than the spin Hall effect in vdW magnets remain scarce. Here, we utilize Cr as the orbital current source to efficiently manipulate the magnetization of the vdW ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2 at room temperature. In the Fe3GaTe2/Pt (1.5 nm)/Cr (4.5 nm) trilayer structure, the orbital current originating from Cr is converted into the spin current via Pt, which then exerts a torque on Fe3GaTe2. Compared with control samples using 6 nm Pt as the spin current source, the switching current density in OHE-based devices is reduced by 3.9 times, resulting in a 52% reduction in power consumption. This work presents the promising potential of harnessing orbital currents to realize energy-efficient 2D SOT-MRAM.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that using Cr as an orbital current source in Fe3GaTe2/Pt/Cr trilayer structures enables more energy-efficient spin-orbit torque switching of the 2D van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2 compared to conventional spin Hall effect-based methods, achieving a 3.9× reduction in switching current density and 52% lower power consumption.
AI.motivation: Conventional spin Hall materials (heavy metals, topological insulators) used for SOT switching in 2D vdW magnets suffer from limitations in torque efficiency and energy consumption. Although orbital Hall conductivity in light metals exceeds spin Hall conductivity, direct experimental evidence of OHE enabling more energy-efficient SOT switching in vdW magnets was lacking.
AI.method: The authors fabricate a Fe3GaTe2/Pt (1.5 nm)/Cr (4.5 nm) trilayer structure, where Cr serves as an orbital current source. The orbital current from Cr is converted into spin current via the Pt interlayer, which then exerts torque on the vdW ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2. Control samples using 6 nm Pt as the spin current source are compared.
AI.result: The OHE-based devices achieved a 3.9× reduction in switching current density and a 52% reduction in power consumption compared to conventional spin Hall effect-based control samples using Pt.
AI.conclusion: Harnessing orbital currents from light metals like Cr presents a promising pathway for realizing energy-efficient 2D SOT-MRAM devices.

title: Physical aging of glasses of an organic semiconductor
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 59 references, Supporting Information (12 figures)
summary: All glasses, including organic semiconductor glasses, are non-equilibrium materials whose properties will change with time. This physical aging process is poorly understood for organic semiconductors, hindering the rational design of highly durable devices. In this study, we investigated the volume and enthalpy recovery processes in both thin films and bulk glasses of N,N'-Bis(3-methylphenyl)-N,N'-diphenylbenzidine (TPD). Our results revealed that volume recovery kinetics exhibit negligible dependence on film thickness for liquid-cooled TPD films between 400 nm and 100 nm. Additionally, the volume recovery process in TPD films was strongly coupled to the enthalpy recovery observed in bulk TPD glasses during annealing near the glass transition temperature. Remarkably, TPD films prepared by physical vapor deposition at room temperature demonstrated exceptional resistance to physical aging, with an aging rate approximately one order of magnitude lower than that of their liquid-cooled counterparts. These results not only enhance our understanding of the non-equilibrium dynamics in amorphous systems but also offer valuable insights for the design of next-generation organic devices with significantly improved stability and durability.

AI.tldr: This study investigates physical aging in TPD organic semiconductor glasses, finding that volume recovery kinetics are thickness-independent for liquid-cooled films (100-400 nm), coupled with enthalpy recovery near Tg, and that vapor-deposited films exhibit ~10x lower aging rates than liquid-cooled ones.
AI.motivation: Physical aging in organic semiconductor glasses is poorly understood, hindering the rational design of highly durable organic devices.
AI.method: Volume and enthalpy recovery processes were investigated in thin films (100-400 nm) and bulk glasses of TPD, comparing liquid-cooled and physically vapor-deposited samples.
AI.result: Volume recovery kinetics show negligible thickness dependence for liquid-cooled TPD films (400 nm to 100 nm); volume recovery is strongly coupled to enthalpy recovery near Tg; vapor-deposited TPD films exhibit aging rates ~10x lower than liquid-cooled counterparts.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance understanding of non-equilibrium dynamics in amorphous systems and provide insights for designing organic devices with improved stability and durability.

title: Best Practices for First-Principles Modeling of Amorphous Oxide Semiconductors: A Statistical Framework and Application to Zn-Sn-O
summary: Ternary and quaternary amorphous oxide semiconductors have many properties that make them promising candidates for use in electronic applications like display, memory, and back end of line logic. However, finding the right material for a given application and optimizing its properties, deposition, and integration, requires a thorough understanding of the physics and chemistry at play. When properly carried out, first principles computations can play a crucial role in enhancing this understanding. In this work, we highlight several pitfalls often observed in research applying these computations, with the Zn-Sn-O system as an example. We show that a proper understanding of the fundamental differences between the physics of the crystalline and amorphous or disordered phases is crucial, as is a proper statistical sampling of structural models. For the Zn-Sn-O system we conclude that from a performance point of view, mobility and initial threshold voltage, it is a promising material class. However, our computed results show that a similar sensitivity to hydrogen induced doping may be present as in IGZO.

AI.tldr: This paper highlights common pitfalls in first-principles computations of amorphous oxide semiconductors using Zn-Sn-O as an example, emphasizing the need to understand differences between crystalline and amorphous physics and proper statistical sampling. It finds Zn-Sn-O promising for electronic applications but notes similar hydrogen-induced doping sensitivity as in IGZO.
AI.motivation: To enhance understanding of ternary/quaternary amorphous oxide semiconductors for electronic applications by identifying and addressing common pitfalls in first-principles computations, using the Zn-Sn-O system as a case study.
AI.method: First-principles computations applied to the Zn-Sn-O system, with emphasis on proper statistical sampling of structural models and understanding fundamental differences between crystalline and amorphous/disordered phase physics.
AI.result: Zn-Sn-O is a promising material class for electronic applications in terms of mobility and initial threshold voltage, but exhibits similar sensitivity to hydrogen-induced doping as IGZO.
AI.conclusion: Proper first-principles computations require understanding crystalline vs. amorphous physics differences and adequate statistical sampling. Zn-Sn-O shows promise but shares hydrogen doping sensitivity with IGZO.
